entries.1e0e668c7d8a7f347d86cbb946d74d348a54bb6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv110"/><title type="x-ms">John</title> <div sID="gen26578" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26579" type="x-p"/> It is not material to enquire when and where this gospel was written; we are sure that it was given by inspiration of God to John, the brother of James, one of the twelve apostles, distinguished by the honourable character of <hi type="italic">that disciple whom Jesus loved,</hi> one of the first three of the worthies of the Son of David, whom he took to be the witnesses of his retirements, particularly of his transfiguration and his agony. The ancients tell us that John lived longest of all the twelve apostles, and was the only one of them that died a natural death, all the rest suffering martyrdom; and some of them say that he wrote this gospel at Ephesus, at the request of the ministers of the several churches of Asia, in opposition to the heresy of Corinthus and the Ebionites, who held that our Lord was a <hi type="italic">mere man.</hi> It seems most probable that he wrote it before his banishment into the isle of Patmos, for there he wrote his <hi type="italic">Apocalypse,</hi> the close of which seems designed for the closing up of the canon of scripture; and, if so, this gospel was not written after. I cannot therefore give credit to those later fathers, who say that he wrote it in his banishment, or after his return from it, many years after the destruction of Jerusalem; when he was ninety years old, saith one of them; when he was a hundred, saith another of them. However, it is clear that he wrote last of the four evangelists, and, comparing his gospel with theirs, we may observe, 1. That he <hi type="italic">relates</hi> what they had <hi type="italic">omitted;</hi> he <hi type="italic">brings up the rear,</hi> and his gospel is as the <hi type="italic">rearward</hi> or <hi type="italic">gathering host;</hi> it gleans up what they has passed by. Thus there was a <hi type="italic">later</hi> collection of Solomon's wise sayings (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.1">Prov. xxv. 1</reference>), and yet far short of what he delivered, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.32">1 Kings iv. 32</reference>. 2. That he gives us more of the <hi type="italic">mystery</hi> of that of which the other evangelists gave us only the <hi type="italic">history.</hi> It was necessary that the matters of fact should be first settled, which was done in their <hi type="italic">declarations of those things which Jesus began both to do and teach,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.1">Luke i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.1">Acts i. 1</reference>. But, this being done out of the mouth of two or three witnesses, <hi type="italic">John goes on to perfection</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.1">Heb. vi. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">not laying again the foundation,</hi> but building upon it, leading us more within the veil. Some of the ancients observe that the other evangelists wrote more of the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ta somatika</hi></hi>—the <hi type="italic">bodily</hi> things of Christ; but John writes of the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ta pneumatika</hi></hi>—the <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> things of the gospel, the life and soul of it; therefore some have called this gospel the <hi type="italic">key of the evangelists.</hi> Here is it that a <hi type="italic">door</hi> is <hi type="italic">opened in heaven,</hi> and the first voice we hear is, <hi type="italic">Come up hither,</hi> come up higher. Some of the ancients, that supposed the four living creatures in John's vision to represent the four evangelists, make John himself to be the <hi type="italic">flying eagle,</hi> so <hi type="italic">high</hi> does he <hi type="italic">soar,</hi> and <hi type="italic">so clearly</hi> does he <hi type="italic">see</hi> into divine and heavenly things. <div eID="gen26579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26580" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26581" type="x-p"/> The scope and design of this chapter is to confirm our faith in Christ as the eternal Son of God, and the true Messiah and Saviour of the world, that we may be brought to receive him, and rely upon him, as our Prophet, Priest, and King, and to give up ourselves to be ruled, and taught, and saved by him. In order to this, we have here, I. An account given of him by the inspired penman himself, fairly laying down, in the beginning, what he designed his whole book should be the proof of (<reference osisRef="John.1.1-John.1.5">ver. 1-5</reference>); and again (<reference osisRef="John.1.10-John.1.14">ver. 10-14</reference>); and again, <reference osisRef="John.1.16-John.1.18">ver. 16-18</reference>. II. The testimony of John Baptist concerning him (<reference osisRef="John.1.6-John.1.9">ver. 6-9</reference>; and again, <reference osisRef="John.1.15">ver. 15</reference>); but most fully and particularly, <reference osisRef="John.1.19-John.1.37">ver. 19-37</reference>. III. His own manifestation of himself to Andrew and Peter (<reference osisRef="John.1.38-John.1.42">ver. 38-42</reference>), to Philip and Nathanael, <reference osisRef="John.1.43-John.1.51">ver. 43-51</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv110"/> <div eID="gen26581" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26580" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divinity of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen26582" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. <hi type="super">2</hi> The same was in the beginning with God. <hi type="super">3</hi> All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made. <hi type="super">4</hi> In him was life; and the life was the light of men. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not. <div eID="gen26582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26583" type="x-p"/> Augustine says (<hi type="italic">de Civitate Dei,</hi> lib. 10, cap. 29) that his friend Simplicius told him he had heard a Platonic philosopher say that these first verses of St. John's gospel were <hi type="italic">worthy to be written in letters of gold.</hi> The learned Francis Junius, in the account he gives of his own life, tells how he was in his youth infected with loose notions in religion, and by the grace of God was wonderfully recovered by reading accidentally these verses in a bible which his father had designedly laid in his way. He says that he observed such a divinity in the argument, such an authority and majesty in the style, that his flesh trembled, and he was struck with such amazement that for a whole day he scarcely knew where he was or what he did; and thence he dates the beginning of his being religious. Let us enquire what there is in those strong lines. The evangelist here lays down the great truth he is to prove, that Jesus Christ is God, one with the Father. Observe, <div eID="gen26583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26584" type="x-p"/> I. Of whom he speaks—<hi type="italic">The Word</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho logos</hi></hi>. This is an idiom peculiar to John's writings. See <reference osisRef="1John.1.1">1 John i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.7">v. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.13">Rev. xix. 13</reference>. Yet some think that Christ is meant by <hi type="italic">the Word</hi> in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">Acts xx. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb. iv. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.2">Luke i. 2</reference>. The Chaldee paraphrase very frequently calls the Messiah <hi type="italic">Memra—the Word of Jehovah,</hi> and speaks of many things in the Old Testament, said to be done by <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi> as done by that <hi type="italic">Word of the Lord.</hi> Even the vulgar Jews were taught that the <hi type="italic">Word of God</hi> was the same with God. The evangelist, in the close of his discourse (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">v. 18</reference>), plainly tells us why he calls Christ <hi type="italic">the Word—because he is the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, and has declared him. Word</hi> is two-fold: <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">logos endiathetos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">word conceived;</hi> and <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">logos prophorikos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">word uttered.</hi> The <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">logos ho eso</hi></hi> and <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho exo</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">ratio</hi> and <hi type="italic">oratio—intelligence</hi> and <hi type="italic">utterance.</hi> 1. There is the <hi type="italic">word conceived,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">thought,</hi> which is the first and only immediate product and conception of the soul (all the operations of which are performed by <hi type="italic">thought</hi>), and it is one with the soul. And thus the second person in the Trinity is fitly called <hi type="italic">the Word;</hi> for he is the <hi type="italic">first-begotten of the Father,</hi> that eternal essential Wisdom which <hi type="italic">the Lord possessed,</hi> as the soul does its thought, <hi type="italic">in the beginning of his way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.22">Prov. viii. 22</reference>. There is nothing we are more sure of than <hi type="italic">that we think,</hi> yet nothing we are more in the dark about than <hi type="italic">how we think;</hi> who can declare the generation of <hi type="italic">thought</hi> in the soul? Surely then the generations and births of the eternal mind may well be allowed to be great mysteries of godliness, the bottom of which we cannot fathom, while yet we adore the depth. 2. There is the <hi type="italic">word uttered,</hi> and this is <hi type="italic">speech,</hi> the chief and most natural indication of the mind. And thus Christ is <hi type="italic">the Word,</hi> for <hi type="italic">by him</hi> God has in <hi type="italic">these last days spoken to us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">Heb. i. 2</reference>), and has directed us to <hi type="italic">hear him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">Matt. xvii. 5</reference>. He has made known God's mind to us, as a man's word or speech makes known his thoughts, as far as he pleases, and no further. Christ is called that <hi type="italic">wonderful speaker</hi> (see notes on <reference osisRef="Dan.8.13">Dan. viii. 13</reference>), the <hi type="italic">speaker of things hidden</hi> and <hi type="italic">strange.</hi> He is <hi type="italic">the Word</hi> speaking <hi type="italic">from</hi> God to us, and <hi type="italic">to God</hi> for us. John Baptist was <hi type="italic">the voice,</hi> but Christ <hi type="italic">the Word:</hi> being <hi type="italic">the Word,</hi> he is <hi type="italic">the Truth,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> the <hi type="italic">faithful Witness</hi> of the mind of God. <div eID="gen26584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26585" type="x-p"/> II. What he saith of him, enough to prove beyond contradiction that <hi type="italic">he is God.</hi> He asserts, <div eID="gen26585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26586" type="x-p"/> 1. His existence in the beginning: <hi type="italic">In the beginning was the Word.</hi> This bespeaks his existence, not only before his incarnation, but before all time. The beginning of time, in which all creatures were produced and brought into being, found this eternal Word in being. The world was <hi type="italic">from</hi> the beginning, but the Word was <hi type="italic">in</hi> the beginning. Eternity is usually expressed by being <hi type="italic">before the foundation of the world.</hi> The eternity of God is so described (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">Ps. xc. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Before the mountains were brought forth.</hi> So <reference osisRef="Prov.8.23">Prov. viii. 23</reference>. The Word had a being before the world had a beginning. He that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the beginning <hi type="italic">never</hi> began, and therefore was <hi type="italic">ever,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">achronos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">without beginning of time.</hi> So Nonnus. <div eID="gen26586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26587" type="x-p"/> 2. His co-existence with the Father: <hi type="italic">The Word was with God, and the Word was God.</hi> Let none say that when we invite them to Christ we would draw them from God, for Christ is <hi type="italic">with God</hi> and <hi type="italic">is God;</hi> it is repeated in <reference osisRef="John.1.2">v. 2</reference>: <hi type="italic">the same,</hi> the very same that we believe in and preach, was <hi type="italic">in the beginning with God,</hi> that is, he was so from eternity. In the beginning the world was <hi type="italic">from God,</hi> as it was created by him; but the Word was <hi type="italic">with God,</hi> as ever with him. The Word was with God, (1.) In respect of <hi type="italic">essence</hi> and <hi type="italic">substance;</hi> for <hi type="italic">the Word was God:</hi> a distinct person or substance, for he was <hi type="italic">with God;</hi> and yet the same in substance, for he <hi type="italic">was God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb. i. 3</reference>. (2.) In respect of <hi type="italic">complacency</hi> and <hi type="italic">felicity.</hi> There was a glory and happiness which Christ had <hi type="italic">with God</hi> before the world was (<reference osisRef="John.17.5">ch. xvii. 5</reference>), the Son infinitely happy in the enjoyment of his Father's bosom, and no less the Father's delight, the Son of his love, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>. (3.) In respect of <hi type="italic">counsel</hi> and <hi type="italic">design.</hi> The mystery of man's redemption by this Word incarnate was <hi type="italic">hid in God</hi> before all worlds, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.9">Eph. iii. 9</reference>. He that undertook to <hi type="italic">bring us to God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1 Pet. iii. 18</reference>) was himself from eternity <hi type="italic">with God;</hi> so that this grand affair of man's reconciliation to God was concerted between the Father and Son from eternity, and they understand one another perfectly well in it, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zech. vi. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. He was <hi type="italic">by him as one brought up with him</hi> for this service, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>. He was <hi type="italic">with God,</hi> and therefore is said to <hi type="italic">come forth from the Father.</hi> <div eID="gen26587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26588" type="x-p"/> 3. His agency in making the world, <reference osisRef="John.1.3">v. 3</reference>. This is here, (1.) Expressly asserted: <hi type="italic">All things were made by him.</hi> He was <hi type="italic">with God,</hi> not only so as to be <hi type="italic">acquainted</hi> with the divine counsels from eternity, but to be <hi type="italic">active</hi> in the divine operations in the beginning of time. <hi type="italic">Then was I by him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>. God made the world <hi type="italic">by a word</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.6">Ps. xxxiii. 6</reference>) and Christ was <hi type="italic">the Word.</hi> By him, not as a subordinate instrument, but as a co-ordinate agent, God <hi type="italic">made the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">Heb. i. 2</reference>), not as the workman cuts by his axe, but as the body sees by the eye. (2.) The contrary is denied: <hi type="italic">Without him was not any thing made that was made,</hi> from the highest angel to the meanest worm. God the Father did nothing without him in that work. Now, [1.] This proves that <hi type="italic">he is God;</hi> for he that <hi type="italic">built all things is God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.3.4">Heb. iii. 4</reference>. The God of Israel often proved himself to be God with this, that he <hi type="italic">made all things:</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.12 Isa.40.28">Isa. xl. 12, 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">xli. 4</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Jer.10.11-Jer.10.12">Jer. x. 11, 12</reference>. [2.] This proves the excellency of the Christian religion, that the author and founder of it is the same that was the author and founder of the world. How excellent must that constitution needs be which derives its institution from him who is the fountain of all excellency! When we worship Christ, we worship him to whom the patriarchs gave honour as the Creator of the world, and on whom all creatures depend. [3.] This shows how well qualified he was for the work of our redemption and salvation. Help was laid upon one that was mighty indeed; for it was laid upon him that made all things; and he is appointed the author of our bliss who was the author of our being. <div eID="gen26588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26589" type="x-p"/> 4. The original of life and light that is in him: <hi type="italic">In him was life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.4">v. 4</reference>. This further proves that he is God, and every way qualified for his undertaking; for, (1.) He has <hi type="italic">life in himself;</hi> not only the <hi type="italic">true God,</hi> but the <hi type="italic">living God.</hi> God is life; he swears by himself when he saith, <hi type="italic">As I live.</hi> (2.) All living creatures have their life in him; not only all the <hi type="italic">matter</hi> of the creation was <hi type="italic">made</hi> by him, but all the <hi type="italic">life</hi> too that is in the creation is derived from him and supported by him. It was the Word of God that produced the <hi type="italic">moving creatures that had life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.1.20">Gen. i. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.25">Acts xvii. 25</reference>. He is that Word by which man lives more than by bread, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.4">Matt. iv. 4</reference>. (3.) Reasonable creatures have their <hi type="italic">light</hi> from him; that <hi type="italic">life</hi> which is <hi type="italic">the light of men</hi> comes from him. Life in man is something greater and nobler than it is in other creatures; it is <hi type="italic">rational,</hi> and not merely <hi type="italic">animal.</hi> When man became a <hi type="italic">living soul,</hi> his life was <hi type="italic">light,</hi> his capacities such as distinguished him from, and dignified him above, the beasts that perish. The <hi type="italic">spirit of a man is the candle of the Lord,</hi> and it was the eternal Word that lighted this candle. The light of reason, as well as the life of sense, is derived from him, and depends upon him. This proves him fit to undertake our salvation; for life and light, spiritual and eternal life and light, are the two great things that fallen man, who lies so much under the power of <hi type="italic">death</hi> and <hi type="italic">darkness,</hi> has need of. From whom may we better expect the light of divine revelation than from him who gave us the light of human reason? And if, when God gave us natural life, that life was in his Son, how readily should we receive the gospel-record, that he hath given us <hi type="italic">eternal</hi> life, and <hi type="italic">that life</hi> too <hi type="italic">is in his Son!</hi> <div eID="gen26589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26590" type="x-p"/> 5. The manifestation of him to the children of men. It might be objected, If this eternal Word was all in all thus in the creation of the world, whence is it that he has been so little taken notice of and regarded? To this he answers (<reference osisRef="John.1.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">The light shines, but the darkness comprehends it not.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen26590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26591" type="x-p"/> (1.) The discovery of the eternal Word to the lapsed world, even before he was manifested in the flesh: <hi type="italic">The light shineth in darkness.</hi> Light is self-evidencing, and will make itself known; this light, whence the light of men comes, hath shone, and doth shine. [1.] The eternal Word, <hi type="italic">as God,</hi> shines in <hi type="italic">the darkness</hi> of <hi type="italic">natural conscience.</hi> Though men by the fall are become <hi type="italic">darkness,</hi> yet that which may be known of God is manifested in them; see <reference osisRef="Rom.1.19-Rom.1.20">Rom. i. 19, 20</reference>. The light of nature is this light shining in darkness. Something of the power of the divine Word, both as <hi type="italic">creating</hi> and as <hi type="italic">commanding,</hi> all mankind have an innate sense of; were it not for this, earth would be a hell, a place of <hi type="italic">utter darkness;</hi> blessed be God, it is not so yet. [2.] The eternal Word, as Mediator, shone in the darkness of the Old-Testament types and figures, and the prophecies and promises which were of the Messiah from the beginning. He that had commanded the light of this world to shine out of darkness was himself long a light <hi type="italic">shining in darkness;</hi> there was a <hi type="italic">veil</hi> upon this <hi type="italic">light,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">2 Cor. iii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen26591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26592" type="x-p"/> (2.) The disability of the degenerate world to receive this discovery: <hi type="italic">The darkness comprehended it not;</hi> the most of men received the grace of God in these discoveries in vain. [1.] The world of mankind <hi type="italic">comprehended not</hi> the natural light that was in their understandings, but became <hi type="italic">vain in their imaginations</hi> concerning the eternal God and the eternal Word, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">Rom. i. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">28</reference>. The darkness of error and sin overpowered and quite eclipsed this light. God <hi type="italic">spoke once, yea twice,</hi> but <hi type="italic">man perceived it not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.14">Job xxxiii. 14</reference>. [2.] The Jews, who had the light of the Old Testament, yet comprehended not Christ in it. As there was a veil upon Moses's face, so there was upon the people's hearts. In the <hi type="italic">darkness</hi> of the types and shadows the light shone; but such as the <hi type="italic">darkness</hi> of their understandings that they could not <hi type="italic">see</hi> it. It was therefore requisite that Christ should come, both to rectify the errors of the Gentile world and to improve the truths of the Jewish church.
entries.d9d5b8dbb11ebe2b210a56fe22acf18997f12662: <div eID="gen26592" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Testimony of John Baptist; Christ's Incarnation.</title> <div sID="gen26593" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> There was a man sent from God, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7">John. 7</reference> The same came for a witness, to bear witness of the Light, that all <hi type="italic">men</hi> through him might believe. <hi type="super">8</hi> He was not that Light, but <hi type="italic">was sent</hi> to bear witness of that Light. <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">That</hi> was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world. <hi type="super">10</hi> He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not. <hi type="super">11</hi> He came unto his own, and his own received him not. <hi type="super">12</hi> But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to them that believe on his name: <hi type="super">13</hi> Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. 14 And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth. <div eID="gen26593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26594" type="x-p"/> The evangelist designs to bring in John Baptist bearing an honourable testimony to Jesus Christ, Now in these verses, before he does this, <div eID="gen26594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26595" type="x-p"/> I. He gives us some account of the witness he is about to produce. His name was <hi type="italic">John,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">gracious;</hi> his conversation was austere, but he was not the less <hi type="italic">gracious.</hi> Now, <div eID="gen26595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26596" type="x-p"/> 1. We are here told concerning him, in general, that he was a <hi type="italic">man sent of God.</hi> The evangelist had said concerning Jesus Christ that he was <hi type="italic">with God</hi> and that he <hi type="italic">was God;</hi> but here concerning John that he was a <hi type="italic">man,</hi> a mere man. God is pleased to speak to us by men like ourselves. John was a <hi type="italic">great man,</hi> but he was a man, a son of man; he was <hi type="italic">sent from God,</hi> he was God's <hi type="italic">messenger,</hi> so he is called, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1">Mal. iii. 1</reference>. God gave him both his mission and his message, both his credentials and his instructions. John wrought no miracle, nor do we find that he had visions and revelations; but the strictness and purity of his life and doctrine, and the direct tendency of both to reform the world, and to revive the interests of God's kingdom among men, were plain indications that he was <hi type="italic">sent of God.</hi> <div eID="gen26596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26597" type="x-p"/> 2. We are here told what his office and business were (<reference osisRef="John.1.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The same came for a witness,</hi> an eye-witness, a leading witness. He came <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eis martyrian</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">for a testimony.</hi> The legal institutions had been long a testimony for God in the Jewish church. By them revealed religion was kept up; hence we read of the <hi type="italic">tabernacle of the testimony, the ark of the testimony, the law and the testimony:</hi> but now divine revelation is to be turned into another channel; now the testimony of Christ is the testimony of God, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">1 Cor. i. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1">ii. 1</reference>. Among the Gentiles, God indeed had not left himself without witness (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Acts xiv. 17</reference>), but the Redeemer had no testimonies borne him among them. There was a profound silence concerning him, till John Baptist came for a witness to him. Now observe, (1.) The matter of his testimony: <hi type="italic">He came to bear witness to the light.</hi> Light is a thing which witnesses for itself, and carries its own evidence along with it; but to those who shut their eyes against the light it is necessary there should be those that bear witness to it. Christ's light needs not man's testimony, but the world's darkness does. John was like the night watchman that goes round the town, proclaiming the approach of the morning light to those that have closed their eyes, and are not willing themselves to observe it; or like that watchman that was set to tell those who asked him what of the night that <hi type="italic">the morning comes,</hi> and, <hi type="italic">if you will enquire, enquire ye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.21.11-Isa.21.12">Isa. xxi. 11, 12</reference>. He was sent of God to tell the world that the long-looked-for Messiah was now come, who should be <hi type="italic">a light to enlighten the Gentiles and the glory of his people Israel;</hi> and to proclaim that dispensation at hand which would bring life and immortality to light. (2.) The design of his testimony: <hi type="italic">That all men through him might believe;</hi> not in him, but in Christ, whose way he was sent to prepare. He taught men to look through him, and pass through him, to Christ; through the doctrine of repentance for sin to that of faith in Christ. He prepared men for the reception and entertainment of Christ and his gospel, by awakening them to a sight and sense of sin; and that, their eyes being thereby opened, they might be ready to admit those beams of divine light which, in the person and doctrine of the Messiah, were now ready to shine in their faces. If they would but receive this witness of man, they would soon find that the witness of God was greater, <reference osisRef="1John.5.9">1 John v. 9</reference>. See <reference osisRef="John.10.41">ch. x. 41</reference>. Observe, it was designed that all men through him might believe, excluding none from the kind and beneficial influences of his ministry that did not exclude themselves, as multitudes did, who rejected the counsel of God against themselves, and so received the grace of God in vain. <div eID="gen26597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26598" type="x-p"/> 3. We are here cautioned not to mistake him for the light who only came to bear witness to it (<reference osisRef="John.1.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">He was not that light</hi> that was expected and promised, but only was sent to bear witness of that great and ruling light. He was a star, like that which guided the wise men to Christ, a morning star; but he was not the Sun; not the Bridegroom, but a friend of the Bridegroom; not the Prince, but his harbinger. There were those who rested in John's baptism, and looked no further, as those Ephesians, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.3">Acts xix. 3</reference>. To rectify this mistake, the evangelist here, when he speaks very honourably of him, yet shows that he must give place to Christ. He was great as the prophet of the Highest, but not the Highest himself. Note, We must take heed of over-valuing ministers, as well as of under-valuing them; they are not our lords, nor have they dominion over our faith, but ministers by whom we believe, stewards of our Lord's house. We must not give up ourselves by an implicit faith to their conduct, for they are not that light; but we must attend to, and receive, their testimony; for they are sent to bear witness of that light; so then let us esteem them, and not otherwise. Had John pretended to be that light he had not been so much as a faithful witness of that light. Those who usurp the honour of Christ forfeit the honour of being the servants of Christ; yet John was very serviceable as a witness to the light, though he was not that light. Those may be of great use to us who yet shine with a borrowed light. <div eID="gen26598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26599" type="x-p"/> II. Before he goes on with John's testimony, he returns to give us a further account of this Jesus to whom John bore record. Having shown in the beginning of the chapter the glories of his Godhead, he here comes to show the graces of his incarnation, and his favours to man as Mediator. <div eID="gen26599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26600" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ was the <hi type="italic">true Light</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.9">v. 9</reference>); not as if John Baptist were a false light, but, in comparison with Christ, he was a very small light. Christ is the great light that deserves to be called so. Other lights are but figuratively and equivocally called so: Christ is the true light. The fountain of all knowledge and of all comfort must needs be the true light. He is the true light, for proof of which we are not referred to the emanations of his glory in the invisible world (the beams with which he enlightens that), but to those rays of his light which are darted downwards, and with which this dark world of ours is enlightened. But how does Christ enlighten every man that comes into the world? (1.) By his creating power he enlightens every man with the light of reason; that life which is the light of men is from him; all the discoveries and directions of reason, all the comfort it gives us, and all the beauty it puts upon us, are from Christ. (2.) By the publication of his gospel to all nations he does in effect enlighten every man. John Baptist was a light, but he enlightened only Jerusalem and Judea, and the region round about Jordan, like a candle that enlightens one room; but Christ is the true light, for he is a light to enlighten the Gentiles. His everlasting gospel is to be preached to every nation and language, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6">Rev. xiv. 6</reference>. Like the sun which enlightens every man that will open his eyes, and receive its light (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">Ps. xix. 6</reference>), to which the preaching of the gospel is compared. See <reference osisRef="Rom.10.18">Rom. x. 18</reference>. Divine revelation is not now to be confined, as it had been, to one people, but to be diffused to all people, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.15">Matt. v. 15</reference>. (3.) By the operation of his Spirit and grace he enlightens all those that are enlightened to salvation; and those that are not enlightened by him perish in darkness. <hi type="italic">The light of the knowledge of the glory of God</hi> is said to be <hi type="italic">in the face of Jesus Christ,</hi> and is compared with that light which was at the beginning commanded to shine out of darkness, and which enlightens every man that comes into the world. Whatever light any man has, he is indebted to Christ for it, whether it be natural or supernatural. <div eID="gen26600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26601" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ <hi type="italic">was in the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.10">v. 10</reference>. He was in the world, as the essential Word, before his incarnation, upholding all things; but this speaks of his being in the world when he took our nature upon him, and dwelt among us; see <reference osisRef="John.16.28">ch. xvi. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">I am come into the world.</hi> The Son of the Highest was here in this <hi type="italic">lower</hi> world; that <hi type="italic">light</hi> in this <hi type="italic">dark</hi> world; that <hi type="italic">holy thing</hi> in this sinful polluted world. He left a world of bliss and glory, and was here in this melancholy miserable world. He undertook to reconcile the world to God, and therefore was <hi type="italic">in the world,</hi> to treat about it, and settle that affair; to satisfy God's justice for the world, and discover God's favour to the world. He was in the world, but not of it, and speaks with an air of triumph when he can say, <hi type="italic">Now I am no more in it,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.11">ch. xvii. 11</reference>. The greatest honour that ever was put upon this world, which is so mean and inconsiderable a part of the universe, was that the Son of God was once <hi type="italic">in the world;</hi> and, as it should engage our affections to things above that there Christ is, so it should reconcile us to our present abode in <hi type="italic">this</hi> world that once Christ was <hi type="italic">here.</hi> He <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the world for awhile, but it is spoken of as a thing past; and so it will be said of us shortly, We were in the world. O that when we are here no more we may be where Christ is! Now observe here, (1.) What reason Christ had to expect the most affectionate and respectful welcome possible in this world; for <hi type="italic">the world was made by him. Therefore</hi> he came to save a lost world because it was a world of his own making. Why should he not concern himself to revive the light that was of his own kindling, to restore a life of his own infusing, and to renew the image that was originally of his own impressing? The world was <hi type="italic">made by him,</hi> and therefore ought to do him homage. (2.) What cold entertainment he met with, notwithstanding: <hi type="italic">The world knew him not.</hi> The great Maker, Ruler, and Redeemer of the world was in it, and few or none of the inhabitants of the world were aware of it. The <hi type="italic">ox knows his owner,</hi> but the more brutish world did not. They did not own him, did not bid him welcome, because they did not <hi type="italic">know him;</hi> and they did not know him because he did not make himself known in the way that they expected—in external glory and majesty. His kingdom came not <hi type="italic">with observation,</hi> because it was to be a kingdom of trail and probation. When he shall come as a Judge the world shall <hi type="italic">know</hi> him. <div eID="gen26601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26602" type="x-p"/> 3. He <hi type="italic">came to his own</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.11">v. 11</reference>); not only to the world, which was <hi type="italic">his own,</hi> but to the people of Israel, that were peculiarly <hi type="italic">his own</hi> above all people; of them he came, among them he lived, and to them he was <hi type="italic">first sent.</hi> The Jews were at this time a mean despicable people; <hi type="italic">the crown was fallen from their head;</hi> yet, in remembrance of the ancient covenant, bad as they were, and poor as they were, Christ was not ashamed to look upon them as his own. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Ta idia</hi></hi>—his own <hi type="italic">things;</hi> not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tous idious</hi></hi>—his own <hi type="italic">persons,</hi> as <hi type="italic">true believers</hi> are called, <reference osisRef="John.13.1">ch. xiii. 1</reference>. The Jews were <hi type="italic">his,</hi> as a man's house, and lands, and goods are <hi type="italic">his,</hi> which he uses and possesses; but believers are his as a man's wife and children are his own, which he loves and enjoys. He came to his own, to seek and save them, because they were <hi type="italic">his own.</hi> He was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, for it was he whose own the sheep were. Now observe, <div eID="gen26602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26603" type="x-p"/> (1.) That the generality <hi type="italic">rejected</hi> him: <hi type="italic">His own received him not.</hi> He had reason to expect that those who were his own should have bidden him welcome, considering how great the <hi type="italic">obligations</hi> were which they <hi type="italic">lay under</hi> to him, and how fair the <hi type="italic">opportunities</hi> were which they had of coming to the knowledge of him. They had the oracles of God, which told them beforehand <hi type="italic">when</hi> and <hi type="italic">where</hi> to expect him, and of what tribe and family he should arise. He came among them himself, introduced with signs and wonders, and himself the greatest; and therefore it is not said of them, as it was of the world (<reference osisRef="John.1.10">v. 10</reference>), that they <hi type="italic">knew him not;</hi> but <hi type="italic">his own,</hi> though they could not but know him, yet <hi type="italic">received him not;</hi> did not receive his doctrine, did not welcome him as the Messiah, but fortified themselves against him. The <hi type="italic">chief priests,</hi> that were in a particular manner <hi type="italic">his own</hi> (for the Levites were God's tribe), were ring-leaders in this contempt put upon him. Now this was very <hi type="italic">unjust,</hi> because they were <hi type="italic">his own,</hi> and therefore he might <hi type="italic">command</hi> their respect; and it was very <hi type="italic">unkind</hi> and <hi type="italic">ungrateful,</hi> because he came to them, to seek and save them, and so to <hi type="italic">court</hi> their respect. Note, Many who in profession are <hi type="italic">Christ's own,</hi> yet do not <hi type="italic">receive him,</hi> because they will not part with their sins, nor have him to <hi type="italic">reign over them.</hi> <div eID="gen26603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26604" type="x-p"/> (2.) That yet there was a remnant who <hi type="italic">owned</hi> him, and were faithful to him. Though his own received him not, yet there were those that <hi type="italic">received</hi> him (<reference osisRef="John.1.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">But as many as received him. Though Israel were not gathered,</hi> yet Christ was <hi type="italic">glorious.</hi> Though the body of that nation persisted and perished in unbelief, yet there were many of <hi type="italic">them</hi> that were wrought upon to submit to Christ, and many more that <hi type="italic">were not of that fold.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen26604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26605" type="x-p"/> [1.] The true Christian's <hi type="italic">description</hi> and <hi type="italic">property;</hi> and that is, that he <hi type="italic">receives Christ,</hi> and <hi type="italic">believes on his name;</hi> the latter explains the former. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To be a Christian indeed is to <hi type="italic">believe on Christ's name;</hi> it is to <hi type="italic">assent</hi> to the gospel discovery, and <hi type="italic">consent</hi> to the gospel proposal, concerning him. His name is <hi type="italic">the Word of God; the King of kings, the Lord our righteousness; Jesus a Saviour.</hi> Now to <hi type="italic">believe</hi> on his name is to <hi type="italic">acknowledge</hi> that he is what these great names bespeak him to be, and to <hi type="italic">acquiesce</hi> in it, that he may be so <hi type="italic">to us. Secondly,</hi> Believing in Christ's name is <hi type="italic">receiving</hi> him as a gift from God. We must receive his doctrine as true and good; receive his law as just and holy; receive his offers as kind and advantageous; and we must receive the image of his grace, and impressions of his love, as the governing principle of our affections and actions. <div eID="gen26605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26606" type="x-p"/> [2.] The true Christian's dignity and privilege are twofold:— <div eID="gen26606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26607" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">privilege of adoption,</hi> which takes them into the number of God's children: <hi type="italic">To them gave he power to become the sons of God.</hi> Hitherto, the adoption pertained to the Jews only (<hi type="italic">Israel is my son, my first-born</hi>); but now, by faith in Christ, Gentiles are the <hi type="italic">children of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.26">Gal. iii. 26</reference>. They have <hi type="italic">power,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">exousian</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">authority;</hi> for no man taketh this power to himself, but he who is <hi type="italic">authorized</hi> by the gospel charter. To them gave he a <hi type="italic">right;</hi> to them gave he this pre-eminence. <hi type="italic">This power have all the saints.</hi> Note, 1. It is the unspeakable privilege of all good Christians, that they are become the <hi type="italic">children of God.</hi> They were by nature children of wrath, children of this world. If they be the <hi type="italic">children of God,</hi> they <hi type="italic">become</hi> so, are <hi type="italic">made</hi> so <hi type="italic">Fiunt, non nascuntur Christiani—Persons are not born Christians, but made such.</hi>—Tertullian. <hi type="italic">Behold what manner of love is this,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.1">1 John iii. 1</reference>. God calls them <hi type="italic">his children,</hi> they call him <hi type="italic">Father,</hi> and are entitled to all the privileges of children, those of their way and those of their home. 2. The privilege of adoption is entirely owing to <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ;</hi> he <hi type="italic">gave</hi> this power to them that believe on his name. God is his Father, and so ours; and it is by virtue of our espousals to him, and union with him, that we stand related to God as a Father. It was in Christ that we were <hi type="italic">predestinated to the adoption;</hi> from him we receive both the character and the Spirit of adoption, and he is the <hi type="italic">first-born among many brethren.</hi> The Son of God became a Son of man, that the sons and daughters of men might become the sons and daughters of God Almighty. <div eID="gen26607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26608" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">privilege of regeneration</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Which were born.</hi> Note, All the children of God are born again; all that are adopted are regenerated. This <hi type="italic">real</hi> change evermore attends that <hi type="italic">relative</hi> one. Wherever God confers the dignity of children, he creates the nature and disposition of children. Men cannot do so when they adopt. Now here we have an account of the original of this new birth. 1. Negatively. (1.) It is not <hi type="italic">propagated</hi> by natural generation from our parents. It is <hi type="italic">not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh,</hi> nor of <hi type="italic">corruptible seed,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.23">1 Pet. i. 23</reference>. Man is called <hi type="italic">flesh and blood,</hi> because thence he has his original: but we do not become the children of God as we become the children of our natural parents. Note, Grace does not run in the blood, as corruption does. Man polluted <hi type="italic">begat a son in his own likeness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.5.3">Gen. v. 3</reference>); but man sanctified and renewed does not beget a son in <hi type="italic">that</hi> likeness. The Jews gloried much in their parentage, and the noble blood that ran in their veins: <hi type="italic">We are Abraham's seed;</hi> and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> to them <hi type="italic">pertained the adoption</hi> because they were born of that blood; but this New-Testament adoption is not founded in any such natural relation. (2.) It is not <hi type="italic">produced</hi> by the natural power of our own will. As it is not of <hi type="italic">blood,</hi> nor of <hi type="italic">the will of the flesh,</hi> so neither is it of the <hi type="italic">will of man,</hi> which labours under a moral impotency of determining itself to that which is good; so that the principles of the divine life are not of our own planting, it is the grace of God that makes us willing to be <hi type="italic">his.</hi> Nor can human laws or writings prevail to sanctify and regenerate a soul; if they could, the new birth would be by the will of man. But, 2. Positively: it is of <hi type="italic">God.</hi> This new birth is owing to the word of God as the means (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.23">1 Pet. i. 23</reference>), and to the Spirit of God as the great and sole author. True believers are <hi type="italic">born of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.9">1 John iii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.1">v. 1</reference>. And this is necessary to their adoption; for we cannot expect the <hi type="italic">love of God</hi> if we have not something of his <hi type="italic">likeness,</hi> nor claim the privileges of adoption if we be not under the power of regeneration. <div eID="gen26608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26609" type="x-p"/> 4. The <hi type="italic">word was made flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.14">v. 14</reference>. This expresses Christ's incarnation more clearly than what went before. By his divine presence he always <hi type="italic">was in the world,</hi> and by his prophets he <hi type="italic">came to his own.</hi> But now that the fulness of time was come he was sent forth after another manner, <hi type="italic">made of a woman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Gal. iv. 4</reference>); God manifested in the flesh, according to the faith and hope of holy Job; <hi type="italic">Yet shall I see God in my flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.19.26">Job xix. 26</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen26609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26610" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">human nature of Christ</hi> with which he was veiled; and that expressed two ways. <div eID="gen26610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26611" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">The word was made flesh. Forasmuch as the children,</hi> who were to become the sons of God, <hi type="italic">were partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb. ii. 14</reference>. The Socinians agree that Christ is both God and man, but they say that he <hi type="italic">was man,</hi> and was <hi type="italic">made a God,</hi> as Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.7.1">Exod. vii. 1</reference>), directly contrary to John here, who saith, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Theos en</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He was God,</hi> but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">sarxegeneto</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He was made flesh.</hi> Compare <reference osisRef="John.1.1">v. 1</reference> with this. This intimates not only that he was really and truly man, but that he subjected himself to the miseries and calamities of the human nature. He was made <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> the meanest part of man. Flesh bespeaks man <hi type="italic">weak,</hi> and he was crucified through <hi type="italic">weakness,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.4">2 Cor. xiii. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Flesh</hi> bespeaks man <hi type="italic">mortal</hi> and <hi type="italic">dying</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.39">Ps. lxxviii. 39</reference>), and Christ was <hi type="italic">put to death in the flesh</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1 Pet. iii. 18</reference>. Nay, <hi type="italic">flesh</hi> bespeaks <hi type="italic">man tainted with sin</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen. vi. 3</reference>), and Christ, though he was perfectly holy and harmless, yet appeared <hi type="italic">in the likeness of sinful flesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Rom. viii. 3</reference>), and was made <hi type="italic">sin for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2 Cor. v. 21</reference>. When Adam had sinned, God said to him, <hi type="italic">Dust thou art;</hi> not only because made out of the dust, but because by sin he was sunk into dust. His fall did, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">somatoun ten psychen</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">turn him</hi> as it were <hi type="italic">all into body,</hi> made him earthly; therefore he that was made a curse for us was made <hi type="italic">flesh,</hi> and <hi type="italic">condemned sin in the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Rom. viii. 3</reference>. Wonder at this, that the eternal Word should be made flesh, when flesh was come into such an ill name; that he who made <hi type="italic">all things</hi> should himself be made flesh, one of the meanest things, and submit to that from which he was at the greatest distance. The voice that ushered in the gospel cried, <hi type="italic">All flesh is grass</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Isa. xl. 6</reference>), to make the Redeemer's love the more wonderful, who, to <hi type="italic">redeem</hi> and <hi type="italic">save</hi> us, was made flesh, and withered as grass; but the <hi type="italic">Word of the Lord,</hi> who was made flesh, <hi type="italic">endures for ever;</hi> when made flesh, he ceased not to be the Word of God. <div eID="gen26611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26612" type="x-p"/> [2.] He <hi type="italic">dwelt among us,</hi> here in this lower world. Having taken upon him the nature of man, he put himself into the place and condition of other men. The Word might have been made flesh, and dwelt among the angels; but, having taken a <hi type="italic">body</hi> of the same mould with ours, in it he came, and resided in the same world with us. He <hi type="italic">dwelt among us,</hi> us worms of the earth, us that he had no need of, us that he got nothing by, us that were <hi type="italic">corrupt</hi> and <hi type="italic">depraved,</hi> and revolted from God. The Lord God came and dwelt even <hi type="italic">among the rebellious,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 18</reference>. He that had dwelt among angels, those noble and excellent beings, came and dwelt <hi type="italic">among us</hi> that are a <hi type="italic">generation of vipers,</hi> us <hi type="italic">sinners,</hi> which was worse to him than David's swelling in Mesech and Kedar, or Ezekiel's dwelling <hi type="italic">among scorpions,</hi> or the church of Pergamus dwelling <hi type="italic">where Satan's seat is.</hi> When we look upon the upper world, the world of spirits, how mean and contemptible does this flesh, this body, appear, which we carry about with us, and this world in which our lot is cast, and how hard is it to a contemplative mind to be reconciled to them! But that the eternal Word was <hi type="italic">made flesh,</hi> was clothed with a body as we are, and dwelt in this world as we do, this has put an honour upon them both, and should make us willing to abide in the flesh while God has any work for us to do; for Christ dwelt in this lower world, bad as it is, till he had finished what he had to do here, <reference osisRef="John.17.4">ch. xvii. 4</reference>. He dwelt <hi type="italic">among</hi> the Jews, that the scripture might be fulfilled, <hi type="italic">He shall dwell in the tents of Shem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.9.27">Gen. ix. 27</reference>. And see <reference osisRef="Zech.2.10">Zech. ii. 10</reference>. Though the Jews were unkind to him, yet he continued to dwell among them; though (as some of the ancient writers tell us) he was invited to better treatment by Abgarus king of Edessa, yet he removed not to any other nation. He <hi type="italic">dwelt</hi> among us. He was in the world, not as a wayfaring man that tarries but for a night, but he <hi type="italic">dwelt</hi> among us, made a long residence, the original word is observable, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eskenosen en hemin</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he dwelt among us,</hi> he dwelt <hi type="italic">as in a tabernacle,</hi> which intimates, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he dwelt here in very <hi type="italic">mean</hi> circumstances, as shepherds that dwell in tents. He did not dwell among us <hi type="italic">as in a palace,</hi> but as in a <hi type="italic">tent;</hi> for he had not where to lay his head, and was always upon the remove. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That his state here was a <hi type="italic">military</hi> state. Soldiers <hi type="italic">dwell in tents;</hi> he had long since proclaimed war with the <hi type="italic">seed of the serpent,</hi> and now he takes <hi type="italic">the field</hi> in person, sets up his standard, and pitches his tent, to prosecute this war. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That his stay among us was not to be perpetual. He dwelt here as <hi type="italic">in a tent,</hi> not as at <hi type="italic">home.</hi> The patriarchs, by dwelling in tabernacles, <hi type="italic">confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on earth,</hi> and sought the better country, and so did Christ, leaving us an example, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.13-Heb.13.14">Heb. xiii. 13, 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> That as of old God dwelt in the tabernacle of Moses, by the shechinah between the cherubim, so now he dwells in the human nature of Christ; that is now the true shechinah, the symbol of God's peculiar presence. And we are to make all our addresses to God through Christ, and from him to receive divine oracles. <div eID="gen26612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26613" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">beams of his divine glory</hi> that <hi type="italic">darted</hi> through this <hi type="italic">veil of flesh: We beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.</hi> The sun is still the fountain of light, though eclipsed or clouded; so Christ was still the brightness of his Father's glory, even when he <hi type="italic">dwelt among us</hi> in this lower world. And how slightly soever the Jews thought of him there were those that saw through the veil. Observe, <div eID="gen26613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26614" type="x-p"/> [1.] Who were the witnesses of this glory: <hi type="italic">we,</hi> his disciples and followers, that conversed most freely and familiarly with him; we among whom he <hi type="italic">dwelt.</hi> Other men discover their weaknesses to those that are most familiar with them, but it was not so with Christ; those that were most intimate with him saw most of his glory. As it was with his <hi type="italic">doctrine,</hi> the disciples knew the mysteries of it, while others had it <hi type="italic">under the veil of parables;</hi> so it was with his <hi type="italic">person,</hi> they saw the glory of his divinity, while others saw only the veil of his human nature. He manifested himself <hi type="italic">to them, and not unto the world.</hi> These witnesses were a competent number, twelve of them, a whole jury of witnesses; men of plainness and integrity, and far from any thing of design or intrigue. <div eID="gen26614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26615" type="x-p"/> [2.] What evidence they had of it: <hi type="italic">We saw it.</hi> They had not their evidence by report, at second hand, but were themselves eye-witnesses of those proofs on which they built their testimony that he was the <hi type="italic">Son of the living God: We saw it.</hi> The word signifies a fixed abiding sight, such as gave them an opportunity of making their observations. This apostle himself explains this: <hi type="italic">What we declare unto you</hi> of the Word of life is what we have <hi type="italic">seen with our eyes,</hi> and what <hi type="italic">we have looked upon,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.1.1">1 John i. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen26615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26616" type="x-p"/> [3.] What the glory was: <hi type="italic">The glory as of the only begotten of the Father.</hi> The glory of the <hi type="italic">Word made flesh</hi> was such a glory as became the only <hi type="italic">begotten Son of God,</hi> and could not be the glory of any other. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Jesus Christ is the only begotten of the Father. Believers are the children of God by the special favour of adoption and the special grace of regeneration. They are in a sense <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">homoiousioi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">of a like nature</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.4">2 Pet. i. 4</reference>), and have the image of his perfections; but Christ is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">homousios</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">of the same nature,</hi> and is the express image of his person, and the Son of God by an eternal generation. Angels are sons of God, but he never said to any of them, <hi type="italic">This day have I begotten thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.5">Heb. i. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He was evidently declared to be the only begotten of the Father, by that which was seen of his glory when he dwelt among us. Though he was in the <hi type="italic">form of a servant,</hi> in respect of outward circumstances, yet, in respect of graces, his form was as that of the <hi type="italic">fourth</hi> in the fiery furnace, <hi type="italic">like the Son of God.</hi> His divine glory appeared in the holiness and heavenliness of his doctrine; in his miracles, which extorted from many this acknowledgment, that he was the <hi type="italic">Son of God;</hi> it appeared in the purity, goodness, and beneficence, of his whole conversation. God's goodness is his glory, and he went about doing good; he spoke and acted in every thing as an incarnate Deity. Perhaps the evangelist had a particular regard to the glory of his <hi type="italic">transfiguration,</hi> of which he was an eye-witness; see <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.16-2Pet.1.18">2 Pet. i. 16-18</reference>. God's calling him his <hi type="italic">beloved Son, in whom he was well pleased,</hi> intimated that he was the <hi type="italic">only begotten of the Father;</hi> but the full proof of this was at his resurrection. <div eID="gen26616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26617" type="x-p"/> [4.] What advantage those he dwelt among had from this. He dwelt among them, <hi type="italic">full of grace and truth.</hi> In the old tabernacle wherein God dwelt was the <hi type="italic">law,</hi> in <hi type="italic">this</hi> was grace; in that were <hi type="italic">types,</hi> in this was <hi type="italic">truth.</hi> The incarnate Word was every way qualified for his undertaking as Mediator; for he was <hi type="italic">full of grace and truth,</hi> the two great things that fallen man stands in need of; and this proved him to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God</hi> as much as the divine power and majesty that appeared in him. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He has a fulness of grace and truth <hi type="italic">for himself;</hi> he had the Spirit without measure. He was full <hi type="italic">of grace,</hi> fully acceptable to his Father, and therefore qualified to intercede for us; and full <hi type="italic">of truth,</hi> fully apprized of the things he was to reveal, and therefore fit to instruct us. He had a fulness of knowledge and a fulness of compassion. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He has a fulness of grace and truth <hi type="italic">for us.</hi> He <hi type="italic">received,</hi> that he might <hi type="italic">give,</hi> and God was well pleased in him, that he might be well pleased with us in him; and this was the <hi type="italic">truth</hi> of the legal <hi type="italic">types.</hi>
entries.84653eb28c22e8433283f01054f76cc4faef96e1: <div eID="gen26617" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">John's Testimony to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen26618" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> John bare witness of him, and cried, saying, This was he of whom I spake, He that cometh after me is preferred before me: for he was before me. <hi type="super">16</hi> And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace. <hi type="super">17</hi> For the law was given by Moses, <hi type="italic">but</hi> grace and truth came by Jesus Christ. 18 No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <div eID="gen26618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26619" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen26619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26620" type="x-p"/> I. The evangelist begins again to give us John Baptist's testimony concerning Christ, <reference osisRef="John.1.15">v. 15</reference>. He had said (<reference osisRef="John.1.8">v. 8</reference>) that he <hi type="italic">came for a witness;</hi> now here he tells us that he did accordingly <hi type="italic">bear witness.</hi> Here, Observe, <div eID="gen26620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26621" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">How he expressed</hi> his testimony: He <hi type="italic">cried,</hi> according to the prediction that he should be <hi type="italic">the voice of one crying.</hi> The Old-Testament prophets cried aloud, to show people their <hi type="italic">sins;</hi> this New-Testament prophet cried aloud, to show people their <hi type="italic">Saviour.</hi> This intimates, (1.) That it was an open <hi type="italic">public</hi> testimony, proclaimed, that all manner of persons might take notice of it, for all are concerned in it. False teachers <hi type="italic">entice secretly,</hi> but wisdom publishes her dictates in the chief places of concourse. (2.) That he was free and hearty in bearing this testimony. He <hi type="italic">cried</hi> as one that was both <hi type="italic">well assured</hi> of the truth to which he witnessed and <hi type="italic">well affected</hi> to it. He that had leaped in his <hi type="italic">mother's womb for joy</hi> of Christ's approach, when newly conceived, does now with a like exultation of spirit <hi type="italic">welcome</hi> his public appearance. <div eID="gen26621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26622" type="x-p"/> 2. What his <hi type="italic">testimony</hi> was. He appeals to what he had said at the beginning of his ministry, when he had directed them to expect one that should <hi type="italic">come after him,</hi> whose forerunner he was, and never intended any other than to lead them to him, and to prepare his way. This he had given them notice of from the first. Note, It is very comfortable to a minister to have the testimony of his conscience for him that he set out in his ministry with honest principles and sincere intentions, with a single eye to the glory and honour of Christ. Now what he had then said he applies to this Jesus whom he had lately baptized, and who was so remarkably owned from heaven: <hi type="italic">This was he of whom I spoke.</hi> John did not tell them that there would shortly appear such a one among them, and then leave them to find him out; but in <hi type="italic">this</hi> he went beyond all the Old-Testament prophets that he particularly specified the person: "<hi type="italic">This was he,</hi> the very man I told you of, and to him all I said is to be accommodated." Now what was it he said? <div eID="gen26622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26623" type="x-p"/> (1.) He had given the preference to this Jesus: <hi type="italic">He that comes after me,</hi> in the time of his birth and public appearance, is preferred before me; he that <hi type="italic">succeeds</hi> me in preaching and making disciples is a more excellent person, upon all accounts; as the prince or peer that <hi type="italic">comes after</hi> is preferred before the harbinger or gentleman-usher that makes way for him. Note, Jesus Christ, who was to be called the <hi type="italic">Son of the Highest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Luke i. 32</reference>), was preferred before John Baptist, who was to be called only the <hi type="italic">prophet of the Highest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.76">Luke i. 76</reference>. John was a minister of the New Testament, but Christ was the Mediator of the New Testament. And observe, though John was a great man, and had a great name and interest, yet he was forward to give the preference to him to whom it belonged. Note, All the ministers of Christ must prefer him and his interest before themselves and their own interests; they will make an ill account <hi type="italic">that seek their own things, not the things of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.21">Phil. ii. 21</reference>. He comes <hi type="italic">after me,</hi> and yet is <hi type="italic">preferred before me.</hi> Note, God dispenses his gifts according to his good pleasure, and many times crosses hands, as Jacob did, preferring the <hi type="italic">younger</hi> before the <hi type="italic">elder.</hi> Paul far outstripped those that were in Christ before him. <div eID="gen26623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26624" type="x-p"/> (2.) He here gives a good reason for it: <hi type="italic">For he was before me,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">protos mou en</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He was my first,</hi> or <hi type="italic">first to me;</hi> he was my first Cause, my original. The <hi type="italic">First</hi> is one of <hi type="italic">God's names,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.6">Isa. xliv. 6</reference>. He is <hi type="italic">before me,</hi> is <hi type="italic">my first,</hi> [1.] In respect of <hi type="italic">seniority:</hi> he was <hi type="italic">before me,</hi> for he was before Abraham, <reference osisRef="John.8.58">ch. viii. 58</reference>. Nay, he was <hi type="italic">before all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.17">Col. i. 17</reference>. I am but of yesterday, he from eternity. It was but in <hi type="italic">those days</hi> that John Baptist came (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.1">Matt. iii. 1</reference>), but the goings forth of our Lord Jesus <hi type="italic">were of old, from everlasting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mic. v. 2</reference>. This proves two natures in Christ. Christ, as man, <hi type="italic">came after</hi> John as to his public appearance; Christ, as God, was <hi type="italic">before him;</hi> and how could he otherwise be before him but by an eternal existence? [2.] In respect of supremacy; for he was <hi type="italic">my prince;</hi> so some princes are called the <hi type="italic">first;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">proton</hi></hi>, "It is he for whose sake and service I am sent: he is my Master, I am his minister and messenger." <div eID="gen26624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26625" type="x-p"/> II. He presently returns again to speak of Jesus Christ, and cannot go on with John Baptist's testimony till <reference osisRef="John.1.19">v. 19</reference>. The <reference osisRef="John.1.16">16th verse</reference> has a manifest connection with <reference osisRef="John.1.14">v. 14</reference>, where the incarnate Word was said to be <hi type="italic">full of grace and truth.</hi> Now here he makes this the matter, not only of our adoration, but of our thankfulness, because <hi type="italic">from that fulness</hi> of his <hi type="italic">we all have received. He received gifts for men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 18</reference>), that he might <hi type="italic">give gifts to men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Eph. iv. 8</reference>. He was filled, that he might <hi type="italic">fill all in all</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.23">Eph. i. 23</reference>), might <hi type="italic">fill our treasures,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Prov. viii. 21</reference>. He has a fountain of fulness overflowing: <hi type="italic">We all have received. All we</hi> apostles; so some. We have received the favour of this apostleship, that is <hi type="italic">grace;</hi> and a fitness for it, that is <hi type="italic">truth.</hi> Or, rather, <hi type="italic">All we</hi> believers; as many as received him (<reference osisRef="John.1.16">v. 16</reference>), received from him. Note, All true believers receive from Christ's fulness; the best and greatest saints cannot live without him, the meanest and weakest may live by him. This excludes proud boasting, that we have nothing but <hi type="italic">we have received it;</hi> and silences perplexing fears, that we want nothing but <hi type="italic">we may receive it.</hi> Let us see what it is that we have received. <div eID="gen26625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26626" type="x-p"/> 1. We have received <hi type="italic">grace for grace.</hi> Our receivings by Christ are all summed up in this one word, <hi type="italic">grace;</hi> we have received <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kai charin</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">even grace,</hi> so great a gift, so rich, so invaluable; we have received <hi type="italic">no less</hi> than grace; this is a gift to be spoken of with an emphasis. It is repeated, <hi type="italic">grace for grace;</hi> for to every stone in this building, as well as <hi type="italic">to the top-stone,</hi> we must cry, <hi type="italic">Grace, grace.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen26626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26627" type="x-p"/> (1.) The blessing received. It is <hi type="italic">grace;</hi> the good will of God towards us, and the good work of God in us. God's good will works the good work, and then the good work qualifies us for further tokens of his good will. As the cistern receives water from the fulness of the fountain, the branches sap from the fulness of the root, and the air light from the fulness of the sun, so we receive grace from the fulness of Christ. <div eID="gen26627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26628" type="x-p"/> (2.) The manner of its reception: <hi type="italic">Grace for grace</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">charin anti charitos</hi></hi>. The phrase is singular, and interpreters put different senses upon it, each of which will be of use to illustrate the unsearchable riches of the grace of Christ. <hi type="italic">Grace for grace</hi> bespeaks, [1.] The <hi type="italic">freeness</hi> of this grace. It is grace for grace' sake; so <hi type="italic">Grotius.</hi> We receive grace, not for <hi type="italic">our sakes</hi> (be it known to us), but even so, Father, <hi type="italic">because it seemed good in thy sight.</hi> It is a <hi type="italic">gift according to grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.12.6">Rom. xii. 6</reference>. It is grace <hi type="italic">to us</hi> for the sake of grace to Jesus Christ. God was well pleased in him, and is therefore well pleased with us in him, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Eph. i. 6</reference>. [2.] The <hi type="italic">fulness</hi> of this grace. <hi type="italic">Grace for grace</hi> is abundance of grace, grace upon grace (so <hi type="italic">Camero</hi>), one grace heaped upon another; as <hi type="italic">skin for skin</hi> is skin after skin, even all that a man has, <reference osisRef="Job.2.4">Job ii. 4</reference>. It is a blessing poured out, that there shall not be room to receive it, <hi type="italic">plenteous redemption:</hi> one grace a pledge of more grace. <hi type="italic">Joseph-He will add.</hi> It is such a fulness as is called <hi type="italic">the fulness of God</hi> which we are filled with. We are not straitened in the grace of Christ, if we be not straitened in our own bosoms. [3.] The <hi type="italic">serviceableness</hi> of this grace. <hi type="italic">Grace for grace</hi> is grace for the promoting and advancing of grace. Grace to be <hi type="italic">exercised</hi> by ourselves; gracious habits for gracious acts. Grace to be <hi type="italic">ministered</hi> to others; gracious vouchsafements for gracious performances: grace is a talent to be traded with. The apostles received grace (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.5">Rom. i. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">Eph. iii. 8</reference>), that they might communicate it, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.10">1 Pet. iv. 10</reference>. [4.] The <hi type="italic">substitution</hi> of New-Testament grace <hi type="italic">in the room and stead</hi> of Old-Testament grace: so <hi type="italic">Beza.</hi> And this sense is confirmed by what follows (<reference osisRef="John.1.17">v. 17</reference>); for the Old Testament had grace in type, the New Testament has grace in truth. There was a grace under the Old Testament, the gospel was preached then (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.8">Gal. iii. 8</reference>); but that grace is superseded, and we have gospel grace instead of it, a <hi type="italic">glory which excelleth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.10">2 Cor. iii. 10</reference>. Discoveries of grace are now more clear, distributions of grace far more plentiful; this is grace instead of grace. [5.] It bespeaks the <hi type="italic">augmentation</hi> and <hi type="italic">continuance of grace. Grace for grace</hi> is one grace to improve, confirm, and perfect another grace. We are changed into the divine image, <hi type="italic">from glory to glory,</hi> from one degree of glorious grace to another, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. Those that have <hi type="italic">true</hi> grace have that for <hi type="italic">more grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.4.6">Jam. iv. 6</reference>. When God gives grace he saith, Take this <hi type="italic">in part;</hi> for he who hath promised will perform. [6.] It bespeaks the <hi type="italic">agreeableness</hi> and <hi type="italic">conformity</hi> of grace in the saints to the grace that is in Jesus Christ; so Mr. <hi type="italic">Clark. Grace for grace</hi> is grace in us answering to grace in him, as the impression upon the wax answers the seal line for line. The grace we receive from Christ <hi type="italic">changes us into the same image</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2 Cor. iii. 18</reference>), the <hi type="italic">image of the Son</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Rom. viii. 29</reference>), the <hi type="italic">image of the heavenly,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.49">1 Cor. xv. 49</reference>. <div eID="gen26628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26629" type="x-p"/> 2. We have received <hi type="italic">grace and truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.17">v. 17</reference>. He had said (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">v. 14</reference>) that Christ was <hi type="italic">full of grace and truth;</hi> now here he says that by him <hi type="italic">grace and truth</hi> came to us. From Christ we <hi type="italic">receive grace;</hi> this is a string he delights to harp upon, he cannot go off from it. Two things he further observes in this verse concerning this grace:—(1.) Its <hi type="italic">preference</hi> above the law of Moses: <hi type="italic">The law was given by Moses,</hi> and it was a glorious discovery, both of God's <hi type="italic">will concerning</hi> man and his <hi type="italic">good will to</hi> man; but the gospel of Christ is a much clearer discovery both of duty and happiness. That which was given by Moses was purely terrifying and threatening, and bound with penalties, a law which could not <hi type="italic">give life, which was</hi> given with abundance of terror (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">Heb. xii. 18</reference>); but that which is given by Jesus Christ is of another nature; it has all the beneficial uses of the law, but not the terror, for it is <hi type="italic">grace:</hi> grace <hi type="italic">teaching</hi> (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.11">Tit. ii. 11</reference>), grace <hi type="italic">reigning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.21">Rom. v. 21</reference>. It is a law, but a remedial law. The endearments of love are the genius of the gospel, not the affrightments of law and the curse. (2.) Its <hi type="italic">connection</hi> with truth: <hi type="italic">grace and truth.</hi> In the gospel we have the discovery of the greatest <hi type="italic">truths</hi> to be embraced by the understanding, as well as of the richest <hi type="italic">grace</hi> to be embraced by the will and affections. It is a <hi type="italic">faithful saying,</hi> and <hi type="italic">worthy of all acceptation;</hi> that is, it is <hi type="italic">grace and truth.</hi> The offers of <hi type="italic">grace</hi> are <hi type="italic">sincere,</hi> and what we may venture our souls upon; they are made <hi type="italic">in earnest,</hi> for it is <hi type="italic">grace and truth.</hi> It is <hi type="italic">grace and truth</hi> with reference to the <hi type="italic">law</hi> that was <hi type="italic">given by Moses.</hi> For it is, [1.] The performance of all the Old-Testament promises. In the Old Testament we often find <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> and <hi type="italic">truth</hi> put together, that is, mercy according to promise; so here <hi type="italic">grace and truth</hi> denote grace according to promise. See <reference osisRef="Luke.1.72">Luke i. 72</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.56">1 Kings viii. 56</reference>. [2.] It is the substance of all the Old-Testament types and shadows. Something of grace there was both in the ordinances that were instituted for Israel and the providences that occurred concerning Israel; but they were only shadows of good things to come, even of the grace that is to be <hi type="italic">brought to us by the revelation of Jesus Christ.</hi> He is the <hi type="italic">true</hi> paschal lamb, the <hi type="italic">true</hi> scape-goat, the true <hi type="italic">manna.</hi> They had grace in the picture; we have grace in the person, that is, <hi type="italic">grace and truth.
