Grace and truth came,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">egeneto</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">was made;</hi> the same word that was used (<reference osisRef="John.1.3">v. 3</reference>) concerning Christ's <hi type="italic">making all things.</hi> The law was only <hi type="italic">made known</hi> by Moses, but the <hi type="italic">being</hi> of this grace and truth, as well as the discovery of them, is owing to Jesus Christ; this was <hi type="italic">made</hi> by him, as the world at first was; and by him this <hi type="italic">grace and truth</hi> do <hi type="italic">consist.</hi> <div eID="gen26629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26630" type="x-p"/> 3. Another thing we receive from Christ is a clear revelation of God to us (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">v. 18</reference>): He hath <hi type="italic">declared</hi> God to us, whom <hi type="italic">no man hath seen at any time.</hi> This was the grace and truth which came by Christ, the knowledge of God and an acquaintance with him. Observe, <div eID="gen26630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26631" type="x-p"/> (1.) The insufficiency of all other discoveries: <hi type="italic">No man hath seen God at any time.</hi> This intimates, [1.] That the nature of God being <hi type="italic">spiritual,</hi> he is invisible to bodily eyes, he is a being <hi type="italic">whom no man hath seen, nor can see,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1 Tim. vi. 16</reference>. We have therefore need to <hi type="italic">live by faith,</hi> by which we <hi type="italic">see him that is invisible,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.27">Heb. xi. 27</reference>. [2.] That the revelation which God made of himself in the Old Testament was very short and imperfect, in comparison with that which he has made by Christ: <hi type="italic">No man hath seen God at any time;</hi> that is, what was seen and known of God before the incarnation of Christ was nothing to that which is now seen and known; life and immortality are now brought to a much clearer light than they were then. [3.] That none of the Old-Testament prophets were so well qualified to make known the mind and will of God to the children of men as our Lord Jesus was, for none of them had <hi type="italic">seen God at any time. Moses beheld the similitude of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.12.8">Num. xii. 8</reference>), but was told that he could not <hi type="italic">see his face,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.33.20">Exod. xxxiii. 20</reference>. But <hi type="italic">this</hi> recommends Christ's holy religion to us that it was founded by one that had seen God, and knew more of his mind than any one else ever did. <div eID="gen26631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26632" type="x-p"/> (2.) The all-sufficiency of the gospel discovery proved from its author: <hi type="italic">The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen26632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26633" type="x-p"/> [1.] How <hi type="italic">fit</hi> he was to make this discovery, and every way qualified for it. He and he alone was <hi type="italic">worthy to take the book, and to open the seals,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9">Rev. v. 9</reference>. For, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He is <hi type="italic">the only-begotten Son;</hi> and who so likely to know the Father as the Son? or in whom is the Father better known than in the Son? <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. He is of the same nature with the Father, so that he who hath <hi type="italic">seen him</hi> hath seen <hi type="italic">the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.9">ch. xiv. 9</reference>. The servant is not supposed to know so well <hi type="italic">what his Lord does</hi> as the Son, <reference osisRef="John.15.15">ch. xv. 15</reference>. Moses was <hi type="italic">faithful as a servant,</hi> but Christ <hi type="italic">as a Son. Secondly,</hi> He is <hi type="italic">in the bosom of the Father.</hi> He had lain in his bosom from eternity. When he was here upon earth, yet still, as God, he was in the bosom of the Father, and thither he returned when he <hi type="italic">ascended. In the bosom of the Father;</hi> that is, 1. In the bosom of his <hi type="italic">special love,</hi> dear to him, in <hi type="italic">whom he was well pleased,</hi> always his delight. All God's saints are <hi type="italic">in his hand,</hi> but his Son was <hi type="italic">in his bosom,</hi> one in nature and essence, and therefore in the highest degree one <hi type="italic">in love.</hi> 2. In the bosom of his <hi type="italic">secret counsels.</hi> As there was a mutual <hi type="italic">complacency,</hi> so there was a mutual <hi type="italic">consciousness,</hi> between the Father and Son (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>); none so fit as he to make known God, for none knew his mind as he did. Our most secret counsels we are said to hide <hi type="italic">in our bosom (in pectore</hi>); Christ was privy to the <hi type="italic">bosom-counsels</hi> of the Father. The prophets <hi type="italic">sat down at his feet</hi> as scholars; Christ lay in his bosom as a friend. See <reference osisRef="Eph.3.11">Eph. iii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen26633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26634" type="x-p"/> [2.] How <hi type="italic">free</hi> he was in making this discovery: <hi type="italic">He hath declared. Him</hi> is not in the original. He has declared that of God which no man had at any time seen or known; not only that which was hid <hi type="italic">of God,</hi> but that which was hid <hi type="italic">in</hi> God (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.9">Eph. iii. 9</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">exegesato</hi></hi>—it signifies a plain, clear, and full discovery, not by general and doubtful hints, but by particular explications. He that runs may now read the will of God and the way of salvation. This is the <hi type="italic">grace,</hi> this the <hi type="italic">truth,</hi> that came by Jesus Christ.
entries.20ccb8d5369c42e8289dd7ea7eca13627490f555: <div eID="gen26634" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">John's Testimony to Christ; John Examined by the Priests.</title> <div sID="gen26635" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> And this is the record of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, Who art thou? 20 And he confessed, and denied not; but confessed, I am not the Christ. <hi type="super">21</hi> And they asked him, What then? Art thou Elias? And he saith, I am not. Art thou that prophet? And he answered, No. <hi type="super">22</hi> Then said they unto him, Who art thou? that we may give an answer to them that sent us. What sayest thou of thyself? <hi type="super">23</hi> He said, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord, as said the prophet Esaias. <hi type="super">24</hi> And they which were sent were of the Pharisees. <hi type="super">25</hi> And they asked him, and said unto him, Why baptizest thou then, if thou be not that Christ, nor Elias, neither that prophet? <hi type="super">26</hi> John answered them, saying, I baptize with water: but there standeth one among you, whom ye know not; <hi type="super">27</hi> He it is, who coming after me is preferred before me, whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose. <hi type="super">28</hi> These things were done in Bethabara beyond Jordan, where John was baptizing. <div eID="gen26635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26636" type="x-p"/> We have here the testimony of John, which he delivered to the messengers who were sent from Jerusalem to examine him. Observe here, <div eID="gen26636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26637" type="x-p"/> I. Who they were that sent to him, and who they were that were sent. 1. They that sent to him were <hi type="italic">the Jews at Jerusalem,</hi> the great sanhedrim or high-commission court, which sat at Jerusalem, and was the representative of the Jewish church, who took cognizance of all matters relating to religion. One would think that they who were the fountains of learning, and the guides of the church, should have, by books, understood the times so well as to know that the Messiah was at hand, and therefore should presently have known him that was his forerunner, and readily embraced him; but, instead of this, they sent messengers to <hi type="italic">cross questions</hi> with him. Secular learning, honour, and power, seldom dispose men's minds to the reception of divine light. 2. They that were sent were, (1.) <hi type="italic">Priests and Levites,</hi> probably members of the council, men of learning, gravity, and authority. John Baptist was himself a priest of the seed of Aaron, and therefore it was not fit that he should be examined by any but priests. It was prophesied concerning John's ministry that it should <hi type="italic">purify the Sons of Levi</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.3">Mal. iii. 3</reference>), and therefore they were jealous of him and his reformation. (2.) They were <hi type="italic">of the Pharisees,</hi> proud, self-justiciaries, that thought they needed no repentance, and therefore could not bear one that made it his business to preach repentance. <div eID="gen26637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26638" type="x-p"/> II. On what errand they were sent; it was to enquire concerning John and <hi type="italic">his baptism.</hi> They did not send for John to them, probably because they <hi type="italic">feared the people,</hi> lest the people where John was should be provoked to rise, or lest the people where they were should be brought acquainted with him; they thought it was good to keep him at a distance. They enquire concerning him, 1. To satisfy their curiosity; as the Athenians enquired concerning Paul's doctrine, for the novelty of it, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.19-Acts.17.20">Acts xvii. 19, 20</reference>. Such a proud conceit they had of themselves that the doctrine of repentance was to them strange doctrine. 2. It was to show their authority. They thought they <hi type="italic">looked great</hi> when they called him to account whom all men counted as a prophet, and arraigned him at their bar. 3. It was with a design to <hi type="italic">suppress</hi> him and silence him if they could find any colour for it; for they were jealous of his growing interest, and his ministry agreed neither with the Mosaic dispensation which they had been long under, nor with the notions they had formed of the Messiah's kingdom. <div eID="gen26638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26639" type="x-p"/> III. What was the answer he gave them, and his account, both concerning himself and concerning his baptism, in both which he witnessed to Christ. <div eID="gen26639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26640" type="x-p"/> 1. Concerning himself, and what he professed himself to be. They asked him, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Sy tis ei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Thou, who art thou?</hi> John's appearing in the world was surprising. He was in the wilderness till the day of his showing unto Israel. His spirit, his converse, he doctrine, had something in them which commanded and gained respect; but he did not, as seducers do, give out himself to be <hi type="italic">some great one.</hi> He was more industrious to <hi type="italic">do good</hi> than to <hi type="italic">appear great;</hi> and therefore waived saying any thing of himself till he was legally interrogated. Those speak best for Christ that say least of themselves, whose <hi type="italic">own works</hi> praise them, not <hi type="italic">their own lips.</hi> He answers their interrogatory, <div eID="gen26640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26641" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Negatively.</hi> He was not that great one whom some took him to be. God's faithful witnesses stand more upon their guard <hi type="italic">against undue respect</hi> than against <hi type="italic">unjust contempt.</hi> Paul writes as warmly against those that overvalued him, and said, <hi type="italic">I am of Paul,</hi> as against those that undervalued him, and said that his bodily presence was weak; and he rent his clothes when he was called a god. [1.] John disowns himself to be <hi type="italic">the Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He said, I am not the Christ,</hi> who was now expected and waited for. Note, The ministers of Christ must remember that <hi type="italic">they are not Christ,</hi> and therefore must not usurp his powers and prerogatives, nor assume the praises due to him only. They are not Christ, and therefore must not lord it over God's heritage, nor pretend to a dominion over the faith of Christians. They cannot created grace and peace; they cannot enlighten, convert, quicken, comfort; for they are not Christ. Observe how emphatically this is here expressed concerning John: He <hi type="italic">confessed, and denied not, but confessed;</hi> it denotes his vehemence and constancy in making this protestation. Note, Temptations to pride, and assuming that honour to ourselves which does not belong to us, ought to be resisted with a great deal of vigour and earnestness. When John was taken to be the Messiah, he did not connive at it with a <hi type="italic">Si populus vult decipi, decipiatur—If the people will be deceived, let them;</hi> but openly and solemnly, without any ambiguities, confessed, <hi type="italic">I am not the Christ;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hoti ouk eimi ego ho Christos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I am not the Christ, not I;</hi> another is at hand, who is he, but I am not. His disowning himself to be the Christ is called his <hi type="italic">confessing</hi> and not <hi type="italic">denying</hi> Christ. Note, Those that humble and abase themselves thereby confess Christ, and give honour to him; but those that will not deny themselves do in effect deny Christ, [2.] He disowns himself to be Elias, <reference osisRef="John.1.21">v. 21</reference>. The Jews expected the person of Elias to return from heaven, and to live among them, and promised themselves great things from it. Hearing of John's character, doctrine, and baptism, and observing that he appeared as one dropped from heaven, in the same part of the country from which Elijah was carried to heaven, it is no wonder that they were ready to take him for this Elijah; but he disowned this honour too. He was indeed prophesied of under the name of Elijah (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.5">Mal. iv. 5</reference>), and he came in the <hi type="italic">spirit and power of Elias</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Luke i. 17</reference>), and was the Elias that was to come (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.14">Matt. xi. 14</reference>); but he was not the person of Elias, not that Elias that went to heaven in the fiery chariot, as he was that met Christ in his transfiguration. He was the Elias that God had promised, not the Elias that they foolishly dreamed of. Elias did come, and <hi type="italic">they knew him not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.12">Matt. xvii. 12</reference>); nor did he make himself known to them as the Elias, because they had promised themselves such an Elias as God never promised them. [3.] He disowns himself to be that <hi type="italic">prophet,</hi> or the prophet. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He was not <hi type="italic">that</hi> prophet which Moses said <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> would <hi type="italic">raise up to them of their brethren,</hi> like unto him. If they meant this, they needed not ask that question, for that prophet was no other than the Messiah, and he had said already, <hi type="italic">I am not the Christ. Secondly,</hi> He was not such a prophet as they expected and wished for, who, like Samuel and Elijah, and some other of the prophets, would interpose in public affairs, and rescue them from under the Roman yoke. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He was not one of the old prophets raised from the dead, as they expected one to come before Elias, as Elias before the Messiah. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Though John was a prophet, yea, more than a prophet, yet he had his revelation, not by dreams and visions, as the Old-Testament prophets had theirs; his commission and work were of another nature, and belonged to another dispensation. If John had said that he was Elias, and was a prophet, he might have made his words good; but ministers must, upon all occasions, express themselves with the utmost caution, both that they may not confirm people in any mistakes, and particularly that they may not give occasion to any to think of them <hi type="italic">above what is meet.</hi> <div eID="gen26641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26642" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Affirmatively.</hi> The committee that was sent to examine him pressed for a positive answer (<reference osisRef="John.1.22">v. 22</reference>), urging the authority of <hi type="italic">those that sent them,</hi> which they expected he should pay a deference to: "<hi type="italic">Tell us, What art thou?</hi> not that we may believe thee, and be baptized by three, but that we may <hi type="italic">give an answer</hi> to those that sent us, and that it may not be said we were sent on a fool's errand." John was looked upon as a man of sincerity, and therefore they believed he would not give an evasive ambiguous answer; but would be fair and above-board, and give a plain answer to a plain question: <hi type="italic">What sayest thou of thyself?</hi> And he did so, <hi type="italic">I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen26642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26643" type="x-p"/> [1.] He gives his answer in the words of scripture, to show that the scripture was fulfilled in him, and that his office was supported by a divine authority. What the scripture saith of the office of the ministry should be often thought of by those of that high calling, who must look upon themselves as that, and that only, which the word of God makes them. <div eID="gen26643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26644" type="x-p"/> [2.] He gives in his answer in very humble, modest, self-denying expressions. He chooses to apply that scripture to himself which denotes not his dignity, but his duty and dependence, which bespeaks him little: <hi type="italic">I am the voice,</hi> as if he were <hi type="italic">vox et præterea nihil</hi>—<hi type="italic">mere voice.</hi> <div eID="gen26644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26645" type="x-p"/> [3.] He gives such an account of himself as might be profitable to them, and might excite and awaken them to hearken to him; for he <hi type="italic">was the voice</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa. xl. 3</reference>), a voice to alarm, an articulate voice to instruct. Ministers are but the <hi type="italic">voice,</hi> the vehicle, by which God is pleased to communicate his mind. What are Paul and Apollos but messengers? Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He was a <hi type="italic">human</hi> voice. The people were prepared to receive the law by the voice of thunders, and a trumpet exceedingly loud, such as made them tremble; but they were prepared for the gospel by the voice of a man like ourselves, <hi type="italic">a still small voice,</hi> such as that in which God came to Elijah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.12">1 Kings xix. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He was the voice of <hi type="italic">one crying,</hi> which denotes, 1. His <hi type="italic">earnestness</hi> and <hi type="italic">importunity</hi> in calling people to repentance; he <hi type="italic">cried aloud, and did not spare.</hi> Ministers must preach as those that are in earnest, and are themselves affected with those things with which they desire to affect others. Those words are not likely to <hi type="italic">thaw</hi> the hearers' hearts that <hi type="italic">freeze</hi> between the speaker's lips. 2. His <hi type="italic">open publication</hi> of the doctrine he preached; he was the voice of one <hi type="italic">crying,</hi> that all manner of persons might hear and take notice. <hi type="italic">Doth not wisdom cry?</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.1">Prov. viii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It was in the <hi type="italic">wilderness</hi> that this voice was crying; in a place of silence and solitude, out of the noise of the world and the hurry of its business; the more retired we are from the tumult of secular affairs the better prepared we are to hear from God. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> That which he cried was, <hi type="italic">Make straight the way of the Lord;</hi> that is, 1. He came to <hi type="italic">rectify</hi> the mistakes of people concerning the ways of God; it is certain that they are right ways, but the scribes and Pharisees, with their corrupt glosses upon the law, had made them crooked. Now John Baptist calls people to return to the original rule. 2. He came to prepare and dispose people for the reception and entertainment of Christ and his gospel. It is an allusion to the harbingers of a prince or great man, that cry, <hi type="italic">Make room.</hi> Note, When God is coming towards us, we must prepare to meet him, and let the word of the Lord have <hi type="italic">free course.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ps.24.7">Ps. xxiv. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen26645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26646" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is his testimony concerning <hi type="italic">his baptism.</hi> <div eID="gen26646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26647" type="x-p"/> (1.) The enquiry which the committee made about it: <hi type="italic">Why baptizest thou, if thou be not the Christ, nor Elias, nor that prophet?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.25">v. 25</reference>. [1.] They readily apprehended baptism to be fitly and properly used as a sacred rite or ceremony, for the Jewish church had used it with circumcision in the admission of proselytes, to signify the cleansing of them from the pollutions of their former state. That sign was made use of in the Christian church, that it might be the more passable. Christ did not affect novelty, nor should his ministers. [2.] They expected it would be used in the days of the Messiah, because it was promised that then there should be a <hi type="italic">fountain opened</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zech. xiii. 1</reference>), and <hi type="italic">clean water sprinkled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.25">Ezek. xxxvi. 25</reference>. It is taken for granted that Christ, and Elias, and <hi type="italic">that prophet,</hi> would baptize, when they came to <hi type="italic">purify</hi> a <hi type="italic">polluted</hi> world. Divine justice drowned the old world <hi type="italic">in its filth,</hi> but divine grace has provided for the cleansing of this new world <hi type="italic">from its filth.</hi> [3.] They would therefore know by what authority John baptized. His denying himself to be Elias, or <hi type="italic">that prophet,</hi> subjected him to this further question, <hi type="italic">Why baptizest thou?</hi> Note, It is no new thing for a man's modesty to be turned against him, and improved to his prejudice; but it is better that men should take advantage of our low thoughts of ourselves, to <hi type="italic">trample upon us,</hi> than the devil take advantage of our high thoughts of ourselves, to <hi type="italic">tempt us</hi> to pride and draw us into his condemnation. <div eID="gen26647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26648" type="x-p"/> (2.) The account he gave of it, <reference osisRef="John.1.26-John.1.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. <div eID="gen26648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26649" type="x-p"/> [1.] He owned himself to be only the minister of the outward sign: "<hi type="italic">I baptize with water,</hi> and that is all; I am no more, and do no more, than what you see; I have no other title than <hi type="italic">John the Baptist;</hi> I cannot confer the spiritual grace signified by it." Paul was in care that none should think of him above what they saw him to be (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.6">2 Cor. xii. 6</reference>); so was John Baptist. Ministers must not set up for masters. <div eID="gen26649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26650" type="x-p"/> [2.] He directed them to one who was greater than himself, and would do that for them, if they pleased, which he could not do: "<hi type="italic">I baptize with water,</hi> and that is the utmost of my commission; I have nothing to do but by this to lead you to one that comes after me, and consign you to him." Note, The great business of Christ's ministers is to direct all people to him; we preach not ourselves, but <hi type="italic">Christ Jesus the Lord.</hi> John gave the same account to this committee that he had given to the people (<reference osisRef="John.1.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">This as he of whom I spoke.</hi> John was constant and uniform in his testimony, not as a reed shaken with the wind. The sanhedrim were jealous of his interest in the people, but he is not afraid to tell them that there is one at the door that will go beyond him. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He tells them of Christ's <hi type="italic">presence among them</hi> now at this time: <hi type="italic">There stands one among you,</hi> at this time, <hi type="italic">whom you know not.</hi> Christ stood among the common people, and was as one of them. Note, 1. Much true worth lies hid in this world; obscurity is often the lot of real excellency. Saints are God's <hi type="italic">hidden ones,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">the world knows them not.</hi> 2. God himself is often nearer to us than we are aware of. <hi type="italic">The Lord</hi> is <hi type="italic">in this place,</hi> and <hi type="italic">I knew it not.</hi> They were gazing, in expectation of the messiah: <hi type="italic">Lo he is here,</hi> or he is there, when the kingdom of God was abroad and already <hi type="italic">among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.17.21">Luke xvii. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He tells them of Christ's <hi type="italic">preference above himself:</hi> He comes <hi type="italic">after me,</hi> and yet is <hi type="italic">preferred before me.</hi> This he had said before; he adds here, "Whose <hi type="italic">shoe-latchet I am not worthy to loose;</hi> I am not fit to be named the same day with him; it is an honour too great for me to pretend to be in the meanest office about him," <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.41">1 Sam. xxv. 41</reference>. Those to whom Christ is precious reckon his service, even the most despised instances of it, an honour to them. See <reference osisRef="Ps.84.10">Ps. lxxxiv. 10</reference>. If so great a man as John accounted himself unworthy of the honour of being near Christ, how unworthy then should we account ourselves! Now, one would think, these chief priests and Pharisees, upon this intimation given concerning the approach of the Messiah, should presently have asked who, and where, this excellent person was; and who more likely to tell them than he who had given them this general notice? No, they did not think this any part of their business or concern; they came to molest John, not to receive any instructions from him: so that their ignorance was <hi type="italic">wilful;</hi> they might have known Christ, and would not. <div eID="gen26650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26651" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Notice is taken of the place where all this was done: <hi type="italic">In Bethabara beyond Jordan,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.28">v. 28</reference>. Bethabara signifies the <hi type="italic">house of passage;</hi> some think it was the very place where Israel passed over Jordan into the land of promise under the conduct of Joshua; there was opened the way into the gospel state by Jesus Christ. It was at a great <hi type="italic">distance</hi> from Jerusalem, beyond Jordan; probably because what he did <hi type="italic">there</hi> would be least offensive to the government. Amos must go prophesy in the country, not near the court; but it was sad that Jerusalem should put so far from her the things that belonged to <hi type="italic">her peace.</hi> He made this confession in the same place where he was <hi type="italic">baptizing,</hi> that all those who attended his baptism might be witnesses of it, and none might say that they knew not what to <hi type="italic">make of him.</hi>
entries.6cf20d6cf526bf7d22296ce82e74485d856590f7: <div eID="gen26651" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">John's Testimony to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen26652" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world. <hi type="super">30</hi> This is he of whom I said, After me cometh a man which is preferred before me: for he was before me. <hi type="super">31</hi> And I knew him not: but that he should be made manifest to Israel, therefore am I come baptizing with water. <hi type="super">32</hi> And John bare record, saying, I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it abode upon him. <hi type="super">33</hi> And I knew him not: but he that sent me to baptize with water, the same said unto me, Upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and remaining on him, the same is he which baptizeth with the Holy Ghost. <hi type="super">34</hi> And I saw, and bare record that this is the Son of God. <hi type="super">35</hi> Again the next day after John stood, and two of his disciples; <hi type="super">36</hi> And looking upon Jesus as he walked, he saith, Behold the Lamb of God! <div eID="gen26652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26653" type="x-p"/> We have in these verses an account of John's testimony concerning Jesus Christ, which he witnessed to his own disciples that followed him. As soon as ever Christ was <hi type="italic">baptized</hi> he was immediately hurried into the wilderness, to be <hi type="italic">tempted;</hi> and there he was forty days. During his absence John had continued to bear testimony to him, and to tell the people of him; but now at last he <hi type="italic">sees Jesus coming to him,</hi> returning from the wilderness of temptation. As soon as that conflict was over Christ immediately returned to John, who was <hi type="italic">preaching</hi> and <hi type="italic">baptizing.</hi> Now Christ was tempted for example and encouragement to us; and this teaches us, 1. That the <hi type="italic">hardships</hi> of a tempted state should engage us to keep close to ordinances; to go into the <hi type="italic">sanctuary of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Ps. lxxiii. 17</reference>. Our combats with Satan should oblige us to keep close to the communion of saints: two are better than one. 2. That the <hi type="italic">honours</hi> of a victorious state must not set us <hi type="italic">above ordinances.</hi> Christ had triumphed over Satan, and been attended by angels, and yet, after all, he returns to the place where John was preaching and baptizing. As long as we are on this side heaven, whatever extraordinary visits of divine grace we may have here at any time, we must still keep close to the ordinary means of grace and comfort, and walk with God in them. Now here are <hi type="italic">two testimonies</hi> borne by John to Christ, but those two <hi type="italic">agree in one.</hi> <div eID="gen26653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26654" type="x-p"/> I. Here is his testimony to Christ on the first day that he saw him coming from the wilderness; and here four things are witnessed by him concerning Christ, when he had him before his eyes:— <div eID="gen26654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26655" type="x-p"/> 1. That he is <hi type="italic">the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.29">v. 29</reference>. Let us learn here, <div eID="gen26655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26656" type="x-p"/> (1.) That Jesus Christ is the <hi type="italic">Lamb of God,</hi> which bespeaks him the great sacrifice, by which atonement is made for sin, and man reconciled to God. Of all the legal sacrifices he chooses to allude to the <hi type="italic">lambs</hi> that were offered, not only because a lamb is an emblem of meekness, and Christ must be led as a <hi type="italic">lamb to the slaughter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">Isa. liii. 7</reference>), but with a special reference, [1.] To the <hi type="italic">daily sacrifice,</hi> which was offered every morning and evening continually, and that was always a <hi type="italic">lamb</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.38">Exod. xxix. 38</reference>), which was a type of Christ, as the everlasting propitiation, whose blood continually speaks. [2.] To the <hi type="italic">paschal lamb,</hi> the blood of which, being sprinkled upon the door-posts, secured the Israelites from the stroke of the destroying angel. Christ is <hi type="italic">our passover,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">1 Cor. v. 7</reference>. He is the Lamb <hi type="italic">of God;</hi> he is appointed by <hi type="italic">him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">Rom. iii. 25</reference>), he was devoted to him (<reference osisRef="John.17.19">ch. xvii. 19</reference>), and he was accepted with him; in him he was well pleased. The lot which fell on the goat that was to be offered for a sin-offering was called the <hi type="italic">Lord's lot</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.8-Lev.16.9">Lev. xvi. 8, 9</reference>); so Christ, who was to make atonement for sin, is called the <hi type="italic">Lamb of God.</hi> <div eID="gen26656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26657" type="x-p"/> (2.) That Jesus Christ, as the <hi type="italic">Lamb of God, takes away the sin of the world.</hi> This was his undertaking; he appeared, to <hi type="italic">put away sin by the sacrifice of himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.26">Heb. ix. 26</reference>. John Baptist had called people to repent of their sins, in order to the remission of them. Now here he shows how and by whom that remission was to be expected, what ground of hope we have that our sins shall be pardoned upon our repentance, though our repentance makes no satisfaction for them. This ground of hope we have—Jesus Christ is <hi type="italic">the Lamb of God.</hi> [1.] He <hi type="italic">takes away sin.</hi> He, being Mediator between God and man, takes away that which is, above any thing, offensive to the <hi type="italic">holiness</hi> of God, and destructive to the <hi type="italic">happiness</hi> of man. He came, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To take away the guilt of sin by the merit of his death, to vacate the judgment, and reverse the attainder, which mankind lay under, by an act of indemnity, of which all penitent obedient believers may claim the benefit. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To take away the power of sin by the Spirit of his grace, so that it shall not have dominion, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.14">Rom. vi. 14</reference>. Christ, as the Lamb of God, washes us from our sins in his own blood; that is, he both <hi type="italic">justifies</hi> and <hi type="italic">sanctifies</hi> us: he <hi type="italic">takes away sin.</hi> He is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho airon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he is taking away</hi> the sin of the world, which denotes it not a single but a continued act; it is his constant work and office to take <hi type="italic">away sin,</hi> which is such a <hi type="italic">work of time</hi> that it will never be completed till time shall be no more. He is always <hi type="italic">taking away</hi> sin, by the continual intercession of his blood in heaven, and the continual influence of his grace on earth. [2.] He takes away the <hi type="italic">sin of the world;</hi> purchases pardon for all those that repent, and believe the gospel, of what country, nation, or language, soever they be. The legal sacrifices had reference only to the sins of Israel, to make atonement for them; but the Lamb of God was offered to be a propitiation for the <hi type="italic">sin of the whole world;</hi> see <reference osisRef="1John.2.2">1 John ii. 2</reference>. This is encouraging to our faith; if Christ takes away the sin of the world, then why not my sin? Christ levelled his force at the main body of sin's army, struck at the root, and aimed at the overthrow, of that <hi type="italic">wickedness</hi> which the <hi type="italic">whole world lay in.</hi> God was in him reconciling the world to himself. [3.] He does this by <hi type="italic">taking it upon himself.</hi> He is the Lamb of God, that <hi type="italic">bears the sin of the world;</hi> so the margin reads it. He bore sin <hi type="italic">for us,</hi> and so bears it <hi type="italic">from us;</hi> he <hi type="italic">bore the sin of many,</hi> as the scape-goat had the sins of Israel put upon his head, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.21">Lev. xvi. 21</reference>. God could have taken away the sin by taking away the sinner, as he took away the sin of the old world; but he has found out a way of abolishing the sin, and yet sparing the sinner, by making his Son <hi type="italic">sin for us.</hi> <div eID="gen26657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26658" type="x-p"/> (3.) That it is our duty, with an eye of faith, to <hi type="italic">behold</hi> the Lamb of God thus taking away the <hi type="italic">sin of the world.</hi> See him taking away sin, and let that increase our hatred of sin, and resolutions against it. Let not us hold that fast which the Lamb of God came to take away: for Christ will either take our sins away or take us away. Let it increase our love to Christ, <hi type="italic">who loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Rev. i. 5</reference>. Whatever God is pleased to take away from us, if withal he take away our sins, we have reason to be thankful, and no reason to complain. <div eID="gen26658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26659" type="x-p"/> 2. That this was he of whom he had spoken before (<reference osisRef="John.1.30-John.1.31">v. 30, 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is he,</hi> this person whom I now point at, you see where he stands, <hi type="italic">this is he of whom I said, After me cometh a man.</hi> Observe, (1.) This honour John had above all the prophets, that, whereas they spoke of him as one that should come, he saw him already come. <hi type="italic">This is he.</hi> He sees him <hi type="italic">now,</hi> he sees him <hi type="italic">nigh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Num. xxiv. 17</reference>. Such a difference there is between present <hi type="italic">faith</hi> and future <hi type="italic">vision.</hi> Now we love one whom we have not seen; then we shall see him whom our souls love, shall see him, and say, This is he of whom I said, <hi type="italic">my Christ,</hi> and <hi type="italic">my all, my beloved,</hi> and <hi type="italic">my friend.</hi> (2.) John calls Christ <hi type="italic">a man;</hi> after me comes a man—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">aner</hi></hi>, a <hi type="italic">strong man:</hi> like <hi type="italic">the man,</hi> the branch, or the <hi type="italic">man of God's right hand.</hi> (3.) He refers to what he had himself said of him before: <hi type="italic">This is he of whom I said.</hi> Note, Those who have said the most honourable things of Christ will never see cause to unsay them; but the more they know him the more they are confirmed in their esteem of him. John still thinks as meanly of himself, and as highly of Christ, as ever. Though Christ appeared not in any external pomp or grandeur, yet John is not ashamed to own, <hi type="italic">This is he whom I</hi> meant, who is <hi type="italic">preferred before me.</hi> And it was necessary that John should thus show them the person, otherwise they could not have believed that one who made so mean a figure should be he of whom John had spoken such great things. (4.) He protests against any confederacy or combination with this Jesus: <hi type="italic">And I knew him not.</hi> Though there was some relation between them (Elisabeth was cousin to the virgin Mary), yet there was no acquaintance at all between them; John had no personal knowledge of Jesus till he saw him come to his baptism. Their manner of life had been different: John had spent his time in the wilderness, in solitude; Jesus at Nazareth, in conversation. There was no correspondence, no interview between them, that the matter might appear to be wholly carried on by the direction and disposal of Heaven, and not by any design or concert of the persons themselves. And as he hereby disowns all collusion, so also all partiality and sinister regard in it; he could not be supposed to favour him as a friend, for there was no friendship or familiarity between them. Nay, as he could not be biassed to speak honourably of him because he was a stranger to him, he was not able to say any thing of him but what he <hi type="italic">received from above,</hi> to which he appeals, <reference osisRef="John.3.27">ch. iii. 27</reference>. Note, They who are taught believe and confess one whom they have not seen, and blessed are they who <hi type="italic">yet have believed.</hi> (5.) The great intention of John's ministry and baptism was to introduce Jesus Christ. That he should be <hi type="italic">made manifest to Israel, therefore am I come baptizing with water.</hi> Observe, [1.] Though John did not know Jesus by face, yet he knew that he should be made manifest. Note, We may know the certainty of that which yet we do not fully know the nature and intention of. We know that the happiness of heaven <hi type="italic">shall be made manifest to Israel,</hi> but cannot describe it. [2.] The general assurance John had that Christ <hi type="italic">should be made manifest</hi> served to carry him with diligence and resolution through his work, though he was kept in the dark concerning particulars: <hi type="italic">Therefore am I come.</hi> Our assurance of the reality of things, though they are unseen, is enough to quicken us to our duty. [3.] God reveals himself to his people by degrees. At first, John knew no more concerning Christ but that he should be made manifest; in confidence of that, he came baptizing, and now he is favoured with a sight of him. They who, upon God's word, believe what they do not see, shall shortly see what they now believe. [4.] The ministry of the word and sacraments is designed for no other end than to lead people to Christ, and to make him more and more manifest. [5.] Baptism with water made way for the manifesting of Christ, as it supposed our corruption and filthiness, and signified our cleansing by him who is the <hi type="italic">fountain opened.</hi> <div eID="gen26659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26660" type="x-p"/> 3. That this was he <hi type="italic">upon whom the Spirit descended from heaven like a dove.</hi> For the confirming of his testimony concerning Christ, he here vouches the extraordinary appearance at his baptism, in which God himself bore witness to him. This was a considerable proof of Christ's mission. Now, to assure us of the truth of it, we are here told (<reference osisRef="John.1.32-John.1.34">v. 32-34</reference>), <div eID="gen26660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26661" type="x-p"/> (1.) That John Baptist saw it: He <hi type="italic">bore record;</hi> did not relate it as a story, but solemnly attested it, with all the seriousness and solemnity of <hi type="italic">witness-bearing.</hi> He made affidavit of it: <hi type="italic">I saw the Spirit descending</hi> from heaven. John could not see the <hi type="italic">Spirit,</hi> but he saw the dove which was a sign and representation of the Spirit. The Spirit came now upon Christ, both to <hi type="italic">make him fit</hi> for his <hi type="italic">work</hi> and to <hi type="italic">make him known</hi> to the <hi type="italic">world.</hi> Christ was notified, not by the descent of a crown upon him, or by a transfiguration, but by the descent of the Spirit as a dove upon him, to qualify him for his undertaking. Thus the first testimony given to the apostles was by the descent of the Spirit upon them. God's children are made manifest by their <hi type="italic">graces;</hi> their glories are reserved for their future state. Observe, [1.] The spirit descended <hi type="italic">from heaven,</hi> for every good and perfect gift is <hi type="italic">from above.</hi> [2.] He descended <hi type="italic">like a dove</hi>—an emblem of meekness, and mildness, and gentleness, which makes him <hi type="italic">fit to teach.</hi> The dove brought the olive-branch of peace, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.11">Gen. viii. 11</reference>. [3.] The Spirit that descended upon Christ <hi type="italic">abode upon him,</hi> as was foretold, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa. xi. 2</reference>. The Spirit did not <hi type="italic">move him at times,</hi> as Samson (<reference osisRef="Judg.13.25">Judg. xiii. 25</reference>), but <hi type="italic">at all times.</hi> The Spirit was given to him <hi type="italic">without measure;</hi> it was his prerogative to have the Spirit always upon him, so that he could at no time be found either <hi type="italic">unqualified</hi> for his work himself or <hi type="italic">unfurnished</hi> for the supply of those that seek to him for his grace. <div eID="gen26661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26662" type="x-p"/> (2.) That he was <hi type="italic">told to expect it,</hi> which very much corroborates the proof. It was not John's bare conjecture, that surely he on whom he saw the Spirit descending was the Son of God; but it was an <hi type="italic">instituted</hi> sign given him before, by which he might certainly know it (<reference osisRef="John.1.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">I knew him not.</hi> He insists much upon this, that he knew no more of him than other people did, otherwise than by revelation. But <hi type="italic">he that sent me to baptize</hi> gave me this sign, <hi type="italic">Upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, the same is he.</hi> [1.] See here what sure grounds John went upon in his ministry and baptism, that he might proceed with all imaginable satisfaction. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He did not run <hi type="italic">without sending:</hi> God <hi type="italic">sent him to baptize.</hi> He had a warrant from heaven for what he did. When a minister's call is clear, his comfort is sure, though his success is not always so. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He did not run <hi type="italic">without speeding;</hi> for, when he was sent to <hi type="italic">baptize with water,</hi> he was directed to one that should <hi type="italic">baptize with the Holy Ghost.</hi> Under this notion John Baptist was taught to expect Christ, as one who would give that repentance and faith which he called people to, and would carry on and complete that blessed structure of which he was now laying the foundation. Note, It is a great comfort to Christ's ministers, in their administration of the outward signs, that he whose ministers they are can confer the grace signified thereby, and so put life, and soul, and power into their ministrations; can speak to the heart what they speak to the ear, and <hi type="italic">breathe</hi> upon the dry bones to which they <hi type="italic">prophesy.</hi> [2.] See what sure grounds he went upon in his designation of the person of the Messiah. God had before given him a sign, as he did to Samuel concerning Saul: "On whom thou shalt see the Spirit descend, <hi type="italic">that same is he.</hi>" This not only prevented any mistakes, but gave him boldness in his testimony. When he had such assurance as this given him, he could speak with assurance. When John was told this before, his expectations could not but be very much raised; and, when the event exactly answered the prediction, his faith could not but be much confirmed: and these things are written that we may believe. <div eID="gen26662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26663" type="x-p"/> 4. That he is <hi type="italic">the Son of God.</hi> This is the conclusion of John's testimony, that in which all the particulars centre, as the <hi type="italic">quod erat demonstrandum—the fact to be demonstrated</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">I saw, and bore record, that this is the Son of God.</hi> (1.) The truth asserted is, <hi type="italic">that this is the Son of God.</hi> The voice from heaven proclaimed, and John subscribed to it, not only that he should baptize with the Holy Ghost by a divine authority, but that he has a divine nature. This was the peculiar Christian creed, that Jesus is the Son of God (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.16">Matt. xvi. 16</reference>), and here is the first framing of it. (2.) John's testimony to it: "<hi type="italic">I saw, and bore record.</hi> Not only I now bear record of it, but I did so as soon as I had seen it." Observe, [1.] What he <hi type="italic">saw</hi> he was forward to <hi type="italic">bear record</hi> of, as they, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.20">Acts iv. 20</reference>: <hi type="italic">We cannot but speak the things which we have seen.</hi> [2.] What he <hi type="italic">bore record</hi> of was what he <hi type="italic">saw.</hi> Christ's witnesses were eye-witnesses, and therefore the more to be credited: they did not speak by hear-say and report, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.16">2 Pet. i. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen26663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26664" type="x-p"/> II. Here is John's testimony to Christ, the next day after, <reference osisRef="John.1.35-John.1.36">v. 35, 36</reference>. Where observe, 1. He took every opportunity that offered itself to lead people to Christ: <hi type="italic">John stood looking upon Jesus as he walked.</hi> It should seem, John was now retired from the multitude, and was in close conversation with <hi type="italic">two</hi> of his disciples. Note, Ministers should not only in their public preaching, but in their private converse, witness to Christ, and serve his interests. He saw Jesus <hi type="italic">walking</hi> at some distance, yet did not go to him himself, because he would shun every thing that might give the least colour to suspect a combination. He was <hi type="italic">looking upon Jesus</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">emblepsas</hi></hi>; he looked stedfastly, and fixed his eyes upon him. Those that would lead others to Christ must be diligent and frequent in the <hi type="italic">contemplation</hi> of him themselves. John had seen Christ before, but now looked upon him, <reference osisRef="1John.1.1">1 John i. 1</reference>. 2. He repeated the same testimony which he had given to Christ the day before, though he could have delivered some other great truth concerning him; but thus he would show that he was uniform and constant in his testimony, and consistent with himself. His doctrine was the same in private that it was in public, as Paul's was, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.20-Acts.20.21">Acts xx. 20, 21</reference>. It is good to have that repeated which we have heard, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">Phil. iii. 1</reference>. The doctrine of Christ's sacrifice for the taking away of the sin of the world ought especially to be insisted upon by all good ministers: Christ, the Lamb of God, <hi type="italic">Christ and him crucified.</hi> 3. He intended this especially for his two disciples that stood with him; he was willing to turn them over to Christ, for to this end he bore witness to Christ in their hearing that they might leave all to follow him, even that they might leave <hi type="italic">him.</hi> He did not reckon that he lost those disciples who went over from him to Christ, any more than the schoolmaster reckons that scholar lost whom he sends to the university. John gathered disciples, not for himself, but for Christ to <hi type="italic">prepare them for the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Luke i. 17</reference>. So far was he from being jealous of Christ's growing interest, that there was nothing he was more desirous of. Humble generous souls will give others their due praise without fear of diminishing themselves by it. What we have of reputation, as well as of other things, will not be the less for our giving every body his own.
entries.fc6c44e6e33b9b4992fdde2f8495644cf44d00ae: <div eID="gen26664" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Call of Andrew and Peter.</title> <div sID="gen26665" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">37</hi> And the two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus. <hi type="super">38</hi> Then Jesus turned, and saw them following, and saith unto them, What seek ye? They said unto him, Rabbi, (which is to say, being interpreted, Master,) where dwellest thou? <hi type="super">39</hi> He saith unto them, Come and see. They came and saw where he dwelt, and abode with him that day: for it was about the tenth hour. <hi type="super">40</hi> One of the two which heard John <hi type="italic">speak,</hi> and followed him, was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. <hi type="super">41</hi> He first findeth his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ. <hi type="super">42</hi> And he brought him to Jesus. And when Jesus beheld him, he said, Thou art Simon the son of Jona: thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone. <div eID="gen26665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26666" type="x-p"/> We have here the turning over of two disciples from John to Jesus, and one of them fetching in a third, and these are the first-fruits of Christ's disciples; see how small the church was in its beginnings, and what the dawning of the day of its great things was. <div eID="gen26666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26667" type="x-p"/> I. Andrew and another with him were the two that John Baptist had directed to Christ, <reference osisRef="John.1.37">v. 37</reference>. Who the other was we are not told; some think that it was Thomas, comparing <reference osisRef="John.21.2">ch. xxi. 2</reference>; others that it was John himself, the penman of this gospel, whose manner it is industriously to conceal his name, <reference osisRef="John.13.23">ch. xiii. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.20.3">and xx. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen26667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26668" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is their readiness to go over to Christ: They <hi type="italic">heard John speak</hi> of Christ as the <hi type="italic">Lamb of God,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">followed Jesus.</hi> Probably they had heard John say the same thing the day before, and then it had not the effect upon them which now it had; see the benefit of repetition, and of private personal converse. They heard him speak of Christ as the <hi type="italic">Lamb of God, that takes away the sin of the world,</hi> and this made them <hi type="italic">follow him.</hi> The strongest and most prevailing argument with a sensible awakened soul to follow Christ is that it is he, and he only, that <hi type="italic">takes away sin.</hi> <div eID="gen26668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26669" type="x-p"/> 2. The kind notice Christ took of them, <reference osisRef="John.1.38">v. 38</reference>. They came behind him; but, though he had his back towards them, he was soon aware of them, and <hi type="italic">turned,</hi> and <hi type="italic">saw them following.</hi> Note, Christ takes early cognizance of the first motions of a soul towards him, and the first step taken in the way to heaven; see <reference osisRef="Isa.64.5">Isa. lxiv. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.20">Luke xv. 20</reference>. He did not stay till they begged leave to speak with him, but spoke first. What communion there is between a soul and Christ, it is he that <hi type="italic">begins the discourse.</hi> He saith unto them, <hi type="italic">What seek ye?</hi> This was not a reprimand for their boldness in intruding into his company: he that came to <hi type="italic">seek us</hi> never checked any for <hi type="italic">seeking</hi> him; but, on the contrary, it is a kind invitation of them into his acquaintance whom he saw bashful and modest: "Come, what have you to say to me? What is your petition? What is your request." Note, Those whose business it is to instruct people in the affairs of their souls should be humble, and mild, and easy of access, and should encourage those that apply to them. The question Christ put to them is what we should all put to ourselves when we begin to follow Christ, and take upon us the profession of his holy religion: "<hi type="italic">What seek ye?</hi> What do we design and desire?" Those that <hi type="italic">follow</hi> Christ, and yet <hi type="italic">seek</hi> the world, or themselves, or the praise of men, deceive themselves. "<hi type="italic">What seek we</hi> in seeking Christ? Do we seek a teacher, ruler, and reconciler? In following Christ, do we seek the favour of God and eternal life?" If our <hi type="italic">eye</hi> be <hi type="italic">single</hi> in this, we are <hi type="italic">full of light.</hi> <div eID="gen26669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26670" type="x-p"/> 3. Their modest enquiry concerning the place of his abode: <hi type="italic">Rabbi, where dwellest thou?</hi> (1.) In calling him <hi type="italic">Rabbi,</hi> they intimated that their design in coming to him was to be <hi type="italic">taught by him; rabbi</hi> signifies a <hi type="italic">master,</hi> a teaching master; the Jews called their doctors, or learned men, <hi type="italic">rabbies.</hi> The word comes from <hi type="italic">rab, multus</hi> or <hi type="italic">magnus,</hi> a <hi type="italic">rabbi,</hi> a <hi type="italic">great man,</hi> and one that, as we say, has <hi type="italic">much in him.</hi> Never was there such a rabbi as our Lord Jesus, such a <hi type="italic">great one,</hi> in whom were <hi type="italic">hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.</hi> These came to Christ to be his scholars, so must all those that apply themselves to him. John had told them that he was the <hi type="italic">Lamb of God;</hi> now this <hi type="italic">Lamb</hi> is worthy to <hi type="italic">take the book and open the seals</hi> as a rabbi, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9">Rev. v. 9</reference>. And, unless we give up ourselves to be ruled and taught by him, he will not <hi type="italic">take away our sins.</hi> (2.) In asking <hi type="italic">where he dwelt,</hi> they intimate a desire to be better acquainted with him. Christ was a stranger in this country, so that they meant where was his <hi type="italic">inn</hi> where he <hi type="italic">lodged;</hi> for there they would attend him at some seasonable time, when he should appoint, to receive instruction from him; they would not press rudely upon him, when it was not proper. Civility and good manners well become those who follow Christ. And, besides, they hoped to have more from him than they could have in a short conference now by the way. They resolved to make a business, not a by-business of conversing with Christ. Those that have had some communion with Christ cannot but desire, [1.] A <hi type="italic">further communion</hi> with him; they follow on to know more of him. [2.] A <hi type="italic">fixed communion</hi> with him; where they may sit down at his feet, and abide by his instructions. It is not enough to take a turn with Christ now and then, but we must <hi type="italic">lodge with him.</hi> <div eID="gen26670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26671" type="x-p"/> 4. The courteous invitation Christ gave them to his lodgings: <hi type="italic">He saith unto them, Come and see.</hi> Thus should good desires towards Christ and communion with him be countenanced. (1.) He invites them to come to his lodgings: the nearer we approach to Christ, the more we see of his beauty and excellency. Deceivers maintain their interest in their followers by keeping them at a distance, but that which Christ desired to recommend him to the esteem and affections of his followers was that they would <hi type="italic">come and see: "Come and see</hi> what a mean lodging I have, what poor accommodations I take up with, that you may not expect any worldly advantage by following me, as they did who made their court to the scribes and Pharisees, and called them rabbin. <hi type="italic">Come and see</hi> what you must count upon if you follow me." See <reference osisRef="Matt.8.20">Matt. viii. 20</reference>. (2.) He invites them to come <hi type="italic">immediately</hi> and without delay. They asked where he lodged, that they might wait upon him at a more convenient season; but Christ invites them immediately to <hi type="italic">come and see;</hi> never in better time than now. Hence learn, [1.] As to others, that it is best taking people when they are in a good mind; strike while the iron is hot. [2.] As to ourselves, that it is wisdom to embrace the present opportunities: <hi type="italic">Now is the accepted time,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2 Cor. vi. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen26671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26672" type="x-p"/> 5. Their cheerful and (no doubt) thankful acceptance of his invitation: <hi type="italic">They came and saw where he dwelt,</hi> and <hi type="italic">abode with him that day.</hi> It had been greater modesty and manners than had done them good if they had refused this offer. (2.) They readily went along with him: <hi type="italic">They came and saw where he dwelt.</hi> Gracious souls cheerfully accept Christ's gracious invitations; as David, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.8">Ps. xxvii. 8</reference>. They enquired not how they might be accommodated with him, but would put that to the venture, and make the best of what they found. It is good being where Christ is, wherever it be. (2.) They were so well pleased with what they found that they <hi type="italic">abode with him that day</hi> ("Master, it is good to be here"); and he bade them welcome. It was about the tenth hour. Some think that John reckons according to the Roman computation, and that it was about ten o'clock in the morning, and they staid with him till night; others think that John reckons as the other evangelists did, according to the Jewish computation, and that it was four o'clock in the afternoon, and they abode with him that night and the next day. Dr. Lightfoot conjectures that this next day that they spent with Christ was a sabbath-day, and, it being late, they could not get home before the sabbath. As it is our duty, wherever we are, to contrive to spend the sabbath as much as may be to our spiritual benefit and advantage, so they are blessed who, by the lively exercises of faith, love, and devotion, spend their sabbaths in communion with Christ. These are Lord's days indeed, <hi type="italic">days of the Son of man.</hi> <div eID="gen26672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26673" type="x-p"/> II. Andrew brought his brother Peter to Christ. If Peter had been the first-born of Christ's disciples, the papists would have made a noise with it: he did indeed afterwards come to be more eminent in gifts, but Andrew had the honour first to be acquainted with Christ, and to be the instrument of bringing Peter to him. Observe, <div eID="gen26673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26674" type="x-p"/> 1. The <hi type="italic">information</hi> which Andrew gave to Peter, with an intimation to come to Christ. <div eID="gen26674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26675" type="x-p"/> (1.) He <hi type="italic">found him: He first finds his own brother Simon;</hi> his finding implies his seeking him. Simon came along with Andrew to attend John's ministry and baptism, and Andrew knew where to look for him. Perhaps the other disciple that was with him went out to seek some friend of his at the same time, but Andrew sped first: <hi type="italic">He first findeth Simon,</hi> who came only to attend on John, but has his expectations out-done; he meets with Jesus. <div eID="gen26675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26676" type="x-p"/> (2.) He told him whom they had found: <hi type="italic">We have found the Messias.</hi> Observe, [1.] he speaks <hi type="italic">humbly;</hi> not, "I have found," assuming the honour of the discovery to himself, but "<hi type="italic">We</hi> have," rejoicing that he had shared with others in it. [2.] He speaks <hi type="italic">exultingly,</hi> and with triumph: <hi type="italic">We have found</hi> that pearl of great price, that true treasure; and, having found it, he proclaims it as those lepers, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.9">2 Kings vii. 9</reference>, for he knows that he shall have never the less in Christ for others sharing. [3.] He speaks <hi type="italic">intelligently: We have found the Messias,</hi> which was more than had yet been said. John had said, <hi type="italic">He is the Lamb of God, and the Son of God,</hi> which Andrew compares with the scriptures of the Old Testament, and, comparing them together, concludes that he is the Messiah promised to the fathers, for it is now that the fulness of time is come. Thus, by <hi type="italic">making God's testimonies his meditation,</hi> he speaks more clearly concerning Christ than ever <hi type="italic">his teacher</hi> had done, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.99">Ps. cxix. 99</reference>. <div eID="gen26676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26677" type="x-p"/> (3.) He <hi type="italic">brought him to Jesus;</hi> would not undertake to instruct him himself, but brought him to the fountain-head, persuaded him to come to Christ and introduced him. Now this was, [1.] An instance of true love to his brother, <hi type="italic">his own</hi> brother, so he is called here, because he was very dear to him. Note, We ought with a particular concern and application to seek the spiritual welfare of those that are related to us; for their relation to us adds both to the <hi type="italic">obligation</hi> and to the <hi type="italic">opportunity</hi> of doing good to their souls. [2.] It was an effect of his day's conversation with Christ. Note, the best evidence of our profiting by the means of grace is the piety and usefulness of our conversation afterwards. Hereby it appeared that Andrew had <hi type="italic">been with Jesus</hi> that he was so full of him, that he had been <hi type="italic">in the mount,</hi> for his face shone. He knew there was enough in Christ for all; and, having tasted that he is gracious, he could not rest till those he loved had tasted it too. Note, True grace hates monopolies, and loves not to eat its morsels alone. <div eID="gen26677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26678" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">entertainment</hi> which Jesus Christ gave to Peter, who was never the less welcome for his being influenced by his brother to come, <reference osisRef="John.1.42">v. 42</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen26678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26679" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ called him by his name: <hi type="italic">When Jesus beheld him, he said, Thou art Simon, the son of Jona.</hi> It should seem that Peter was utterly a stranger to Christ, and if so, [1.] It was a proof of Christ's omniscience that upon the first sight, without any enquiry, he could tell the name both of him and of his father. <hi type="italic">The Lord knows them that are his,</hi> and their whole case. However, [2.] It was an instance of his condescending grace and favour, that he did thus freely and affably call him by his name, though he was of mean extraction, and <hi type="italic">vir mullius nominis—a man of no name.</hi> It was an instance of God's favour to Moses that he <hi type="italic">knew him by name,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.33.17">Exod. xxxiii. 17</reference>. Some observe the signification of these names: <hi type="italic">Simon</hi>—<hi type="italic">obedient, Jona</hi>—<hi type="italic">a dove.</hi> An obedient dove-like spirit qualifies us to be the disciples of Christ. <div eID="gen26679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26680" type="x-p"/> (2.) He gave him a new name: <hi type="italic">Cephas.</hi> [1.] His giving him a name intimates <hi type="italic">Christ's favour</hi> to him. A new name denotes some great dignity, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.17">Rev. ii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.2">Isa. lxii. 2</reference>. By this Christ not only wiped off the reproach of his mean and obscure parentage, but adopted him into his family as one of his own. [2.] The name which he gave him bespeaks his <hi type="italic">fidelity</hi> to Christ: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be called Cephas</hi> (that is Hebrew for <hi type="italic">a stone), which is by interpretation Peter;</hi> so it should be rendered, as <reference osisRef="Acts.9.36">Acts ix. 36</reference>. <hi type="italic">Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas;</hi> the former Hebrew, the latter Greek, for a <hi type="italic">young roe.</hi> Peter's natural temper was stiff, and hardy, and resolute, which I take to be the principal reason why Christ called him <hi type="italic">Cephas—a stone.</hi> When Christ afterwards prayed for him, that his faith might not fail, that so he might be firm to Christ himself, and at the same time bade him <hi type="italic">strengthen his brethren,</hi> and lay out himself for the support of others, then he <hi type="italic">made him</hi> what he here called him, <hi type="italic">Cephas—a stone.</hi> Those that come to Christ must come with a fixed resolution to be firm and constant to him, <hi type="italic">like a stone,</hi> solid and stedfast; and it is by his grace that they are so. His saying, <hi type="italic">Be thou steady,</hi> makes them so. Now this does no more prove that Peter was the singular or only rock upon which the church is built than the calling of James and John <hi type="italic">Boanerges</hi> proves them the only <hi type="italic">sons of thunder,</hi> or the calling of Joses <hi type="italic">Barnabas</hi> proves him the only <hi type="italic">son of consolation.</hi>
entries.094159b153e5eeee76c84eb8f7979e1456a4e723: <div eID="gen26680" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Call of Philip and Nathanael.</title> <div sID="gen26681" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">43</hi> The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me. <hi type="super">44</hi> Now Philip was of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. 45 Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. <hi type="super">46</hi> And Nathanael said unto him, Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him, Come and see. <hi type="super">47</hi> Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile! <hi type="super">48</hi> Nathanael saith unto him, Whence knowest thou me? Jesus answered and said unto him, Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee. <hi type="super">49</hi> Nathanael answered and saith unto him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel. <hi type="super">50</hi> Jesus answered and said unto him, Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig tree, believest thou? thou shalt see greater things than these. <hi type="super">51</hi> And he saith unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. <div eID="gen26681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26682" type="x-p"/> We have here the call of Philip and Nathanael. <div eID="gen26682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26683" type="x-p"/> I. Philip was called immediately by Christ himself, not as Andrew, who was directed to Christ by John, or Peter, who was invited by his brother. God has various methods of bringing his chosen ones home to himself. But, whatever means he <hi type="italic">uses,</hi> he is not <hi type="italic">tied</hi> to any. 1. Philip was called in a <hi type="italic">preventing</hi> was: <hi type="italic">Jesus findeth Philip.</hi> Christ sought us, and found us, before we made any enquiries after him. The name <hi type="italic">Philip</hi> is of Greek origin, and much used among the Gentiles, which some make an instance of the degeneracy of the Jewish church at this time, and their conformity to the nations; yet Christ changed not his name. 2. He was called the <hi type="italic">day following.</hi> See how closely Christ applied himself to his business. When work is to be done for God, we must not <hi type="italic">lose a day.</hi> Yet observe, Christ now called one or two a day; but, after the Spirit was poured out, there were thousands a day effectually called, in which was fulfilled <reference osisRef="John.14.12">ch. xiv. 12</reference>. 3. Jesus <hi type="italic">would go forth into Galilee</hi> to call him. Christ will find out all those that are given to him, wherever they are, and none of them shall be lost. 4. Philip was brought to be a disciple by the power of Christ going along with that word, <hi type="italic">Follow me.</hi> See the nature of true Christianity; it is <hi type="italic">following Christ,</hi> devoting ourselves to his <hi type="italic">converse</hi> and <hi type="italic">conduct,</hi> attending his movements, and treading in his steps. See the efficacy of the grace of it is the <hi type="italic">rod of his strength.</hi> 5. We are told that Philip was of Bethsaida, and Andrew and Peter were so too, <reference osisRef="John.1.44">v. 44</reference>. These eminent disciples received not honour from the place of their nativity, but reflected honour upon it. <hi type="italic">Bethsaida</hi> signifies the <hi type="italic">house of nets,</hi> because inhabited mostly by fishermen; thence Christ chose disciples, who were to be furnished with extraordinary gifts, and therefore needed not the ordinary advantages of learning. Bethsaida was a wicked place (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.21">Matt. xi. 21</reference>), yet even <hi type="italic">there</hi> was a remnant, according to the election of grace. <div eID="gen26683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26684" type="x-p"/> II. Nathanael was invited to Christ by Philip, and much is said concerning him. In which we may observe, <div eID="gen26684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26685" type="x-p"/> 1. What passed between Philip and Nathanael, in which appears an observable mixture of pious zeal with weakness, such as is usually found in beginners, that are yet but <hi type="italic">asking the way to Zion.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen26685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26686" type="x-p"/> (1.) The joyful news that Philip brought to Nathanael, <reference osisRef="John.1.45">v. 45</reference>. As Andrew before, so Philip here, having got some knowledge of Christ himself, rests not till he has <hi type="italic">made manifest the savour of that knowledge.</hi> Philip, though newly come to an acquaintance with Christ himself, yet steps aside to seek Nathanael. Note, When we have the fairest opportunities of getting good to our own souls, yet ever then we must seek opportunities of doing good to the souls of others, remembering the words of Christ, <hi type="italic">It is more blessed to give than to receive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.35">Acts xx. 35</reference>. O, saith Philip, <hi type="italic">we have found him of whom Moses and the prophets did write,</hi> Observe here, [1.] What a transport of joy Philip was in, upon this new acquaintance with Christ: "We have found him whom we have so often talked of, so long wished and waited for; at last, <hi type="italic">he is come he is come,</hi> and <hi type="italic">we</hi> have found him!" [2.] What an advantage it was to him that he was so well acquainted with the scriptures of the Old Testament, which prepared his mind for the reception of evangelical light, and made the entrance of it much the more easy: <hi type="italic">Him of whom Moses and the prophets did write.</hi> What was written entirely and from eternity in the <hi type="italic">book of the divine counsels</hi> was in part, at sundry times and in divers manners, copied out into the book of the <hi type="italic">divine revelations.</hi> Glorious things were written there concerning the Seed of the woman, the Seed of Abraham, Shiloh, the prophet like Moses, the Son of David, Emmanuel, the Man, the Branch, Messiah the Prince. Philip had studied these things, and was full of them, which made him readily welcome Christ. [3.] What mistakes and weaknesses he laboured under: he called Christ <hi type="italic">Jesus of Nazareth,</hi> whereas he was of <hi type="italic">Bethlehem;</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Son of Joseph,</hi> whereas he as but his <hi type="italic">supposed</hi> Son. Young beginners in religion are subject to mistakes, which time and the grace of God will rectify. It was his weakness to say, <hi type="italic">We have found him,</hi> for Christ found them before they found Christ. He did not yet <hi type="italic">apprehend,</hi> as Paul did, how he was <hi type="italic">apprehended of Christ Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.12">Phil. iii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen26686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26687" type="x-p"/> (2.) The objection which Nathanael made against this, <hi type="italic">Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.46">v. 46</reference>. Here, [1.] His <hi type="italic">caution</hi> was commendable, that he did not lightly assent to every thing that was said, but took it into examination; our rule is, <hi type="italic">Prove all things.</hi> But, [2.] His objection arose from Ignorance. If he meant that no good thing could come out of Nazareth it was owing to his ignorance of the divine grace, as if that were less affected to one place than another, or tied itself to men's foolish and ill-natured observations. If he meant that the Messiah, that great good thing, could not come out of Nazareth, so far he was right (Moses, in the law, said that he should come out of Judah, and the prophets had assigned Bethlehem for the place of his nativity); but then he was ignorant of the matter of <hi type="italic">fact,</hi> that this Jesus was born at Bethlehem; so that the blunder Philip made, in calling him <hi type="italic">Jesus of Nazareth,</hi> occasioned this objection. Note, The mistakes of preachers often give rise to the prejudices of hearers. <div eID="gen26687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26688" type="x-p"/> (3.) The short reply which Philip gave to this objection: <hi type="italic">Come and see.</hi> [1.] It was his <hi type="italic">weakness</hi> that he could not give a satisfactory answer to it; yet it is the common case of young beginners in religion. We may <hi type="italic">know</hi> enough to <hi type="italic">satisfy</hi> ourselves, and yet not be able to <hi type="italic">say</hi> enough to <hi type="italic">silence</hi> the cavils of a subtle adversary. [2.] It was his <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> and zeal that, when he could not answer the objection himself, he would have him go to one that could: <hi type="italic">Come and see.</hi> Let us not stand arguing here, and raising difficulties to ourselves which we cannot get over; let us go and converse with Christ himself, and these difficulties will all vanish presently. Note, It is folly to spend that time in doubtful disputation which might be better spent, and to much better purpose, in the exercises of piety and devotion. <hi type="italic">Come and see;</hi> not, <hi type="italic">Go and see,</hi> but, "<hi type="italic">Come,</hi> and I will go along with thee;" as <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.1.5">Jer. i. 5</reference>.
