From this parley between Philip and Nathanael, we may observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That many people are kept from the ways of religion by the unreasonable prejudices they have conceived against religion, upon the account of some foreign circumstances which do not at all touch the merits of the case. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The best way to remove the prejudices they have entertained against religion is to prove themselves, and make trial of it. Let us not answer this matter before we hear it. <div eID="gen26688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26689" type="x-p"/> 2. What passed between Nathanael and our Lord Jesus. He came and <hi type="italic">saw,</hi> not in vain. <div eID="gen26689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26690" type="x-p"/> (1.) Our Lord Jesus bore a very honourable testimony to Nathanael's integrity: <hi type="italic">Jesus saw him</hi> coming, and met him with favourable encouragement; he said of him to those about him, Nathanael himself being within hearing, <hi type="italic">Behold an Israelite indeed.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen26690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26691" type="x-p"/> [1.] That he <hi type="italic">commended</hi> him; not to flatter him, or puff him up with a good conceit of himself, but perhaps because he knew him to be a <hi type="italic">modest</hi> man, if not a <hi type="italic">melancholy</hi> man, one that had hard and mean thoughts of himself, was ready to doubt his own sincerity; and Christ by this testimony put the matter out of doubt. Nathanael had, more than any of the candidates, objected against Christ; but Christ hereby showed that he excused it, and was not extreme to mark what he had said amiss, because he knew his heart was upright. He did not retort upon him, <hi type="italic">Can any good thing come out of Cana</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.21.2">ch. xxi. 2</reference>), an obscure town in Galilee? But kindly gives him this character, to encourage us to hope for acceptance with Christ, notwithstanding our weakness, and to teach us to speak honourably of those who without cause have spoken slightly of us, and to give them their due praise. <div eID="gen26691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26692" type="x-p"/> [2.] That he commended him for his <hi type="italic">integrity. First, Behold an Israelite indeed.</hi> It is Christ's prerogative to know what men are <hi type="italic">indeed;</hi> we can but <hi type="italic">hope the best.</hi> The whole nation were Israelites in name, but <hi type="italic">all are not Israel that are of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.6">Rom. ix. 6</reference>); here, however, was <hi type="italic">an Israelite indeed.</hi> 1. A sincere follower of the good example of Israel, whose character it was that he was a <hi type="italic">plain man,</hi> in opposition to Esau's character of a <hi type="italic">cunning man.</hi> He was a genuine son of <hi type="italic">honest Jacob,</hi> not only of his <hi type="italic">seed,</hi> but of his <hi type="italic">spirit.</hi> 2. A sincere professor of the faith of Israel; he was true to the religion he professed, and lived up to it: he was really as good as he seemed, and his practice was <hi type="italic">of a piece</hi> with his profession. He is the Jew that is one <hi type="italic">inwardly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>), so is he <hi type="italic">the Christian. Secondly,</hi> He is one in whom is <hi type="italic">no guile</hi>—that is the character of an Israelite indeed, a Christian indeed: <hi type="italic">no guile</hi> towards men; a man without trick or design; a man that one may trust; <hi type="italic">no guile</hi> towards God, that is, sincere in his repentance for sin; sincere in his covenanting with God; in whose spirit is <hi type="italic">no guile,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.2">Ps. xxxii. 2</reference>. He does not say without <hi type="italic">guilt,</hi> but without <hi type="italic">guile.</hi> Though in many things he is foolish and forgetful, yet in nothing false, nor <hi type="italic">wickedly departing from God:</hi> there is no allowed approved guilt in him; not painted, though he have his spots: "<hi type="italic">Behold</hi> this Israelite <hi type="italic">indeed.</hi>" 1. "Take notice of him, that you may learn his way, and do like him." 2. "Admire him; <hi type="italic">behold,</hi> and <hi type="italic">wonder.</hi>" The hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees had so leavened the Jewish church and nation, and their religion was so degenerated into formality or state-policy, that an Israelite indeed was a <hi type="italic">man wondered at,</hi> a miracle of divine grace, like Job, <reference osisRef="John.1.8">ch. i. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen26692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26693" type="x-p"/> (2.) Nathanael is much surprised at this, upon which Christ gives him a further proof of his omnisciency, and a kind memorial of his former devotion. <div eID="gen26693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26694" type="x-p"/> [1.] Here is Nathanael's modesty, in that he was soon put out of countenance at the kind notice Christ was pleased to take of him: "<hi type="italic">Whence knowest thou me,</hi> me that am unworthy of thy cognizance? <hi type="italic">who am I, O Lord God?</hi>" <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18">2 Sam. vii. 18</reference>. This was an evidence of his sincerity, that he did not catch at the praise he met with, but declined it. Christ knows us better than we know ourselves; we know not what is in a man's heart by looking in his face, but all things are naked and open before Christ, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12-Heb.4.13">Heb. iv. 12, 13</reference>. Doth Christ know us? Let us covet to know him. <div eID="gen26694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26695" type="x-p"/> [2.] Here is Christ's further <hi type="italic">manifestation</hi> of himself to him: <hi type="italic">Before Philip called thee, I saw thee. First,</hi> He gives him to understand that he <hi type="italic">knew him,</hi> and so manifests his divinity. It is God's prerogative infallibly to know all persons and all things; by this Christ proved himself to be God upon many occasions. It was prophesied concerning the Messiah that he should be of <hi type="italic">quick understanding in the fear of the Lord,</hi> that is, in judging the sincerity and degree of the fear of God in others, and that he should not <hi type="italic">judge after the sight of his eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2-Isa.11.3">Isa. xi. 2, 3</reference>. Here he answers that prediction. See <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2 Tim. ii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That before Philip called him he saw him under the fig-tree; this manifests a particular kindness for him. 1. His eye was towards him before Philip called him, which was the first time that ever Nathanael was acquainted with Christ. Christ has knowledge of us before we have any knowledge of him; see <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4">Isa. xlv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Gal. iv. 9</reference>. 2. His eye was upon him when he as <hi type="italic">under the fig-tree;</hi> this was a private token which nobody understood but Nathanael: "When thou wast retired <hi type="italic">under the fig-tree</hi> in thy garden, and thoughtest that no eye saw thee, I have then my eye upon thee, and saw that which was very acceptable." It is most probable that Nathanael under the fig-tree was employed, as Isaac in the field, in meditation, and prayer, and communion with God. Perhaps then and there it was that he solemnly joined himself to the Lord in an inviolable covenant. Christ saw in secret, and by this public notice of it did in part reward him openly. <hi type="italic">Sitting under the</hi> fig-tree denotes quietness and composedness of spirit, which much befriend communion with God. See <reference osisRef="Mic.4.4">Mic. iv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.10">Zech. iii. 10</reference>. Nathanael here in was an Israelite indeed, that, like Israel, he <hi type="italic">wrestled with God alone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.24">Gen. xxxii. 24</reference>), prayed not like the hypocrites, in the corners of the streets, but under the fig-tree. <div eID="gen26695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26696" type="x-p"/> (3.) Nathanael hereby obtained a full assurance of faith in Jesus Christ, expressed in that noble acknowledgment (<reference osisRef="John.1.49">v. 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">Rabbi, thou art the Son of God, thou art the king of Israel;</hi> that is, in short, thou art the true Messiah. Observe here, [1.] How <hi type="italic">firmly</hi> he believed <hi type="italic">with the heart.</hi> Though he had lately laboured under some prejudices concerning Christ, they had now all vanished. Note, The grace of God, in working faith, casts down imaginations. Now he asks no more, <hi type="italic">Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?</hi> For he believes Jesus of Nazareth to be the chief good, and embraces him accordingly. [2.] How <hi type="italic">freely</hi> he confessed <hi type="italic">with the mouth.</hi> His confession is made in form of an adoration, directed to our Lord Jesus himself, which is a proper way of confessing our faith. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He confesses Christ's prophetical office, in calling him <hi type="italic">Rabbi,</hi> a title which the Jews commonly gave to their teachers. Christ is the great rabbi, at whose feet we must all be <hi type="italic">brought up. Secondly,</hi> He confesses his divine nature and mission, in calling him the Son of God (that Son of God spoken of <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Ps. ii. 7</reference>); though he had but a human <hi type="italic">form</hi> and <hi type="italic">aspect,</hi> yet having a divine knowledge, the knowledge of the heart, and of things distant and secret, Nathanael thence concludes him to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God. Thirdly,</hi> He confesses, "<hi type="italic">Thou art the king of Israel;</hi> that king of Israel whom we have been long waiting for." If he be the Son of God, he is king of the Israel of God. Nathanael hereby proves himself an Israelite indeed that he so readily owns and submits to the king of Israel. <div eID="gen26696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26697" type="x-p"/> (4.) Christ hereupon raises the hopes and expectations of Nathanael to something further and greater than all this, <reference osisRef="John.1.50-John.1.51">v. 50, 51</reference>. Christ is very tender of young converts, and will encourage good beginnings, though weak, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.20">Matt. xii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen26697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26698" type="x-p"/> [1.] He here signifies his acceptance, and (it should seem) his admiration, of the ready faith of Nathanael: <hi type="italic">Because I said, I saw thee under the fig-tree, believest thou?</hi> He wonders that such a small indication of Christ's divine knowledge should have such an effect; it was a sign that Nathanael's heart was prepared beforehand, else the work had not been done so suddenly. Note, It is much for the honour of Christ and his grace, when the heart is surrendered to him at the first summons. <div eID="gen26698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26699" type="x-p"/> [2.] He promises him much greater helps for the confirmation and increase of his faith than he had had for the first production of it. <div eID="gen26699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26700" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In general: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt see greater things than these,</hi> stronger proofs of my being the Messiah;" the miracles of Christ, and his resurrection. Note, 1. To him that hath, and maketh good use of what he hath, more shall be given. 2. Those who truly believe the gospel will find its evidences grow upon them, and will see more and more cause to believe it. 3. Whatever discoveries Christ is pleased to make of himself to his people while they are here in this world, he hath still greater things than these to make known to them; a glory yet further <hi type="italic">to be revealed.</hi> <div eID="gen26700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26701" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In particular: "Not thou only, but you, all you my disciples, whose faith this is intended for the confirmation of, you <hi type="italic">shall see heaven opened;</hi>" this is more than telling Nathanael of his being under the fig-tree. This is introduced with a solemn preface, <hi type="italic">Verily, verily I say unto you,</hi> which commands both a <hi type="italic">fixed attention</hi> to what is said as very weighty, and a <hi type="italic">full assent</hi> to it as undoubtedly true: "I say it, whose word you may rely upon, <hi type="italic">amen, amen.</hi>" None used this word at the beginning of a sentence but Christ, though the Jews often used it at the close of a prayer, and sometimes doubled it. It is a solemn asseveration. Christ is called the <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.14">Rev. iii. 14</reference>), and so some take it here, <hi type="italic">I the Amen, the Amen, say unto you.</hi> I the faithful witness. Note, The assurances we have of the glory to be revealed are built upon the word of Christ. Now see what it is that Christ assures them of: <hi type="italic">Hereafter,</hi> or <hi type="italic">within awhile,</hi> or <hi type="italic">ere long,</hi> or henceforth, ye shall see heaven opened. <div eID="gen26701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26702" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> It is a mean title that Christ here takes to himself: <hi type="italic">The Son of man;</hi> a title frequently applied to him in the gospel, but always by himself. Nathanael had called him the <hi type="italic">Son of God</hi> and <hi type="italic">king of Israel:</hi> he calls himself <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) To express his <hi type="italic">humility</hi> in the midst of the honours done him. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) To teach his <hi type="italic">humanity,</hi> which is to be believed as well as his divinity. (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) To intimate his present state of humiliation, that Nathanael might not expect this king of Israel to appear in external pomp. <div eID="gen26702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26703" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Yet they are great things which he here foretels: <hi type="italic">You shall see heaven opened,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.</hi> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Some understand it literally, as pointing at some particular event. Either, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] There was some vision of Christ's glory, in which this was exactly fulfilled, which Nathanael was an eye-witness of, as Peter, and James, and John were of his transfiguration. There were many things which Christ did, and those in the presence of his disciples, which were not written (<reference osisRef="John.20.30">ch. xx. 30</reference>), and why not this? Or, [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] It was fulfilled in the many ministrations of the angels to our Lord Jesus, especially that at his ascension, when heaven was opened to receive him, and the angels <hi type="italic">ascended</hi> and <hi type="italic">descended,</hi> to attend him and to do him honour, and this in the sight of the disciples. Christ's ascension was the great proof of his mission, and much confirmed the faith of his disciples, <reference osisRef="John.6.62">ch. vi. 62</reference>. Or, [<hi type="italic">c.</hi>] It may refer to Christ's second coming, to judge the world, when the heavens shall be <hi type="italic">open,</hi> and every eye shall see him, and the angels of God shall ascend and descend about him, as attendants on him, every one employed; and a busy day it will be. See <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.10">2 Thess. i. 10</reference>. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Others take it figuratively, as speaking of a state or series of things to commence <hi type="italic">from henceforth;</hi> and so we may understand it, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] Of Christ's <hi type="italic">miracles.</hi> Nathanael believed, because Christ, as the prophets of old, could tell him things secret; but what is this? Christ is now beginning a dispensation of miracles, much more great and strange than this, as if heaven were opened; and such a power shall be exerted by the Son of man as if the angels, which excel in strength, were continually attending his orders. Immediately after this, Christ began to work miracles, <reference osisRef="John.2.11">ch. ii. 11</reference>. Or, [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] Of his <hi type="italic">mediation,</hi> and that blessed intercourse which he hath settled between heaven and earth, which his disciples should be degrees be let into the mystery of. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By Christ, as Mediator, they shall see <hi type="italic">heaven opened,</hi> that we may <hi type="italic">enter into the holiest</hi> by his blood (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.19-Heb.10.20">Heb. x. 19, 20</reference>); heaven opened, that by faith we may <hi type="italic">look in,</hi> and at length may <hi type="italic">go in;</hi> may now behold the glory of the Lord, and hereafter enter into the joy of our Lord. And, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They shall <hi type="italic">see angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man.</hi> Through Christ we have communion with and benefit by the holy angels, and things in heaven and things on earth are <hi type="italic">reconciled</hi> and <hi type="italic">gathered together.</hi> Christ is to us as Jacob's ladder (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.12">Gen. xxviii. 12</reference>), by whom angels continually ascend and descend for the good of the saints.  <chapter eID="John.1"/> <div eID="gen26703" type="x-p"/>

entries.114bcf4ebda7290bed17586ee91c0477d3d3d2be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14827"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen28612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The author of the Fourth Gospel was the younger of the two sons of Zebedee, a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee, who resided at Bethsaida, where were born Peter and Andrew his brother, and Philip also. His mother's name was Salome, who, though not without her imperfections (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.20-Matt.20.28">Mt 20:20-28</reference>), was one of those dear and honored women who accompanied the Lord on one of His preaching circuits through Galilee, ministering to His bodily wants; who followed Him to the cross, and bought sweet spices to anoint Him after His burial, but, on bringing them to the grave, on the morning of the First Day of the week, found their loving services gloriously superseded by His resurrection ere they arrived. His father, Zebedee, appears to have been in good circumstances, owning a vessel of his own and having hired servants (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.20">Mr 1:20</reference>). Our Evangelist, whose occupation was that of a fisherman with his father, was beyond doubt a disciple of the Baptist, and one of the two who had the first interview with Jesus. He was called while engaged at his secular occupation (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.21">Mt 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.22">22</reference>), and again on a memorable occasion (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.1-Luke.5.11">Lu 5:1-11</reference>), and finally chosen as one of the Twelve Apostles (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.2">Mt 10:2</reference>). He was the youngest of the Twelve--</hi>the "Benjamin," as Da Costa calls him--and he and James his brother were named in the native tongue by Him who knew the heart, "Boanerges," which the Evangelist Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.17">Mr 3:17</reference>) explains to mean "Sons of thunder"; no doubt from their natural vehemence of character. They and Peter constituted that select triumvirate of whom see on <reference osisRef="Luke.9.28">Lu 9:28</reference>. But the highest honor bestowed on this disciple was his being admitted to the bosom place with his Lord at the table, as "the disciple whom Jesus loved" (<reference osisRef="John.13.23">Joh 13:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.2">20:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.21.7">21:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.20.24">20:24</reference>), and to have committed to him by the dying Redeemer the care of His mother (<reference osisRef="John.19.26">Joh 19:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.19.27">27</reference>). There can be no reasonable doubt that this distinction was due to a sympathy with His own spirit and mind on the part of John which the all-penetrating Eye of their common Master beheld in none of the rest; and although this was probably never seen either in his life or in his ministry by his fellow apostles, it is brought out wonderfully in his writings, which, in Christ-like spirituality, heavenliness, and love, surpass, we may freely say, all the other inspired writings.<div eID="gen28612" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28611" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28613" type="x-p"/> After the effusion of the Spirit on the day of Pentecost, we find him in constant but silent company with Peter, the great spokesman and actor in the infant Church until the accession of Paul. While his love to the Lord Jesus drew him spontaneously to the side of His eminent servant, and his chastened vehemence made him ready to stand courageously by him, and suffer with him, in all that his testimony to Jesus might cost him, his modest humility, as the youngest of all the apostles, made him an admiring listener and faithful supporter of his brother apostle rather than a speaker or separate actor. Ecclesiastical history is uniform in testifying that John went to Asia Minor; but it is next to certain that this could not have been till after the death both of Peter and Paul; that he resided at Ephesus, whence, as from a center, he superintended the churches of that region, paying them occasional visits; and that he long survived the other apostles. Whether the mother of Jesus died before this, or went with John to Ephesus, where she died and was buried, is not agreed. One or two anecdotes of his later days have been handed down by tradition, one at least bearing marks of reasonable probability. But it is not necessary to give them here. In the reign of Domitian (A.D. 81-96) he was banished to "the isle that is called Patmos" (a small rocky and then almost uninhabited island in the Ægean Sea), "for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.9">Re 1:9</reference>). Irenæus and Eusebius say that this took place about the end of Domitian's reign. That he was thrown into a cauldron of boiling oil, and miraculously delivered, is one of those legends which, though reported by Tertullian and Jerome, is entitled to no credit. His return from exile took place during the brief but tolerant reign of Nerva; he died at Ephesus in the reign of Trajan [Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, 3.23], at an age above ninety, according to some; according to others, one hundred; and even one hundred twenty, according to others still. The intermediate number is generally regarded as probably the nearest to the truth.<div eID="gen28613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">As to the date of this Gospel, the arguments for its having been composed before the destruction of Jerusalem (though relied on by some superior critics) are of the slenderest nature; such as the expression in <reference osisRef="John.5.2">Joh 5:2</reference>, "there is at Jerusalem, by the sheep-gate, a pool," &c.; there being no allusion to Peter's martyrdom as having occurred according to the prediction in <reference osisRef="John.21.18">Joh 21:18</reference>--</hi>a thing too well known to require mention. That it was composed long after the destruction of Jerusalem, and after the decease of all the other apostles, is next to certain, though the precise time cannot be determined. Probably it was before his banishment, however; and if we date it between the years 90 and 94, we shall probably be close to the truth.<div eID="gen28614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28615" type="x-p"/> As to the readers for whom it was more immediately designed, that they were Gentiles we might naturally presume from the lateness of the date; but the multitude of explanations of things familiar to every Jew puts this beyond all question.<div eID="gen28615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28616" type="x-p"/> No doubt was ever thrown upon the genuineness and authenticity of this Gospel till about the close of the eighteenth century; nor were these embodied in any formal attack upon it till Bretschneider, in 1820, issued his famous treatise [Probabilia], the conclusions of which he afterwards was candid enough to admit had been satisfactorily disproved. To advert to these would be as painful as unnecessary; consisting as they mostly do of assertions regarding the Discourses of our Lord recorded in this Gospel which are revolting to every spiritual mind. The Tubingen school did their best, on their peculiar mode of reasoning, to galvanize into fresh life this theory of the post-Joannean date of the Fourth Gospel; and some Unitarian critics still cling to it. But to use the striking language of Van Oosterzee regarding similar speculations on the Third Gospel, "Behold, the feet of them that shall carry it out dead are already at the door" (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.9">Ac 5:9</reference>). Is there one mind of the least elevation of spiritual discernment that does not see in this Gospel marks of historical truth and a surpassing glory such as none of the other Gospels possess, brightly as they too attest their own verity; and who will not be ready to say that if not historically true, and true just as it stands, it never could have been by mortal man composed or conceived?<div eID="gen28616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Of the peculiarities of this Gospel, we note here only two. The one is its reflective character. While the others are purely narrative, the Fourth Evangelist, "pauses, as it were, at every turn," as Da Costa says [Four Witnesses, p. 234], "at one time to give a reason, at another to fix the attention, to deduce consequences, or make applications, or to give utterance to the language of praise." See <reference osisRef="John.2.20">Joh 2:20</reference>, 21, 23-25; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>, 2; 7:37-39; 11:<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.13">12, 13</reference>, 49-52; 21:18, 19, 22, 23. The other peculiarity of this Gospel is its supplementary character. By this, in the present instance, we mean something more than the studiousness with which he omits many most important particulars in our Lord's history, for no conceivable reason but that they were already familiar as household words to all his readers, through the three preceding Gospels, and his substituting in place of these an immense quantity of the richest matter not found in the other Gospels. We refer here more particularly to the nature of the additions which distinguish this Gospel; particularly the notices of the different Passovers which occurred during our Lord's public ministry, and the record of His teaching at Jerusalem, without which it is not too much to say that we could have had but a most imperfect conception either of the duration of His ministry or of the plan of it. But another feature of these additions is quite as noticeable and not less important. "We find," to use again the words of Da Costa [Four Witnesses, pp. 238, 239], slightly abridged, "only six of our Lord's miracles recorded in this Gospel, but these are all of the most remarkable kind, and surpass the rest in depth, specialty of application, and fulness of meaning. Of these six we find only one in the other three Gospels--</hi>the multiplication of the loaves. That miracle chiefly, it would seem, on account of the important instructions of which it furnished the occasion (<reference osisRef="John.6.1-John.6.71">Joh 6:1-71</reference>), is here recorded anew. The five other tokens of divine power are distinguished from among the many recorded in the three other Gospels by their furnishing a still higher display of power and command over the ordinary laws and course of nature. Thus we find recorded here the first of all the miracles that Jesus wrought--the changing of water into wine (<reference osisRef="John.2.1-John.2.11">Joh 2:1-11</reference>), the cure of the nobleman's son at a distance (<reference osisRef="John.4.43-John.4.54">Joh 4:43-54</reference>); of the numerous cures of the lame and the paralytic by the word of Jesus, only one--of the man impotent for thirty and eight years (<reference osisRef="John.5.1-John.5.9">Joh 5:1-9</reference>); of the many cures of the blind, one only--of the man born blind (<reference osisRef="John.9.1-John.9.12">Joh 9:1-12</reference>); the restoration of Lazarus, not from a deathbed, like Jairus' daughter, nor from a bier, like the widow of Nain's son, but from the grave, and after lying there four days, and there sinking into corruption (<reference osisRef="John.11.1-John.11.44">Joh 11:1-44</reference>); and lastly, after His resurrection, the miraculous draught of fishes on the Sea of Tiberias (<reference osisRef="John.21.5-John.21.11">Joh 21:5-11</reference>). But these are all recorded chiefly to give occasion for the record of those astonishing discourses and conversations, alike with friends and with foes, with His disciples and with the multitude which they drew forth."<div eID="gen28617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28618" type="x-p"/> Other illustrations of the peculiarities of this Gospel will occur, and other points connected with it be adverted to, in the course of the Commentary.<div eID="gen28618" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.1.1-John.1.14">Joh 1:1-14</reference>. The Word Made Flesh.</title> <div sID="gen28619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14827"/><hi type="bold">1. In the beginning--</hi>of all time and created existence, for this Word gave it being (<reference osisRef="John.1.3">Joh 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>); therefore, "before the world was" (<reference osisRef="John.17.5">Joh 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.24">24</reference>); or, from all eternity.<div eID="gen28619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was the Word--</hi>He who is to God what man's word is to himself, the manifestation or expression of himself to those without him. (See on <reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>). On the origin of this most lofty and now for ever consecrated title of Christ, this is not the place to speak. It occurs only in the writings of this seraphic apostle.<div eID="gen28620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was with God--</hi>having a conscious personal existence distinct from God (as one is from the person he is "with"), but inseparable from Him and associated with Him (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.5">Joh 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.1.2">1Jo 1:2</reference>), where "THE Father" is used in the same sense as "God" here.<div eID="gen28621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was God--</hi>in substance and essence God; or was possessed of essential or proper divinity. Thus, each of these brief but pregnant statements is the complement of the other, correcting any misapprehensions which the others might occasion. Was the Word eternal? It was not the eternity of "the Father," but of a conscious personal existence distinct from Him and associated with Him. Was the Word thus "with God?" It was not the distinctness and the fellowship of another being, as if there were more Gods than one, but of One who was Himself God--in such sense that the absolute unity of the God head, the great principle of all religion, is only transferred from the region of shadowy abstraction to the region of essential life and love. But why all this definition? Not to give us any abstract information about certain mysterious distinctions in the Godhead, but solely to let the reader know who it was that in the fulness of time "was made flesh." After each verse, then, the reader must say, "It was He who is thus, and thus, and thus described, who was made flesh." <div eID="gen28622" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b3898ae2a634b75c69f28153e15cec04fb76c8f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14828"/><div sID="gen28623" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14828"/><hi type="bold">2. The same, &c.--</hi>See what property of the Word the stress is laid upon--His eternal distinctness, in unity, from God--the Father (<reference osisRef="John.1.2">Joh 1:2</reference>). <div eID="gen28623" type="x-p"/>
entries.fff0e54479891ca7c1a928a782fd71535b64513c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14829"/><div sID="gen28624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14829"/><hi type="bold">3. All things, &c.--</hi>all things absolutely (as is evident from <reference osisRef="John.1.10">Joh 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.6">1Co 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>; but put beyond question by what follows).<div eID="gen28624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without Him was not any thing--</hi>not one thing.<div eID="gen28625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made--</hi>brought into being.<div eID="gen28626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that was made--</hi>This is a denial of the eternity and non-creation of matter, which was held by the whole thinking world outside of Judaism and Christianity: or rather, its proper creation was never so much as dreamt of save by the children of revealed religion. <div eID="gen28627" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1ea8fe23a27186624ac89f21b3e90272f8cf962: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14830"/><div sID="gen28628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14830"/><hi type="bold">4. In Him was life--</hi>essentially and originally, as the previous verses show to be the meaning. Thus He is the Living Word, or, as He is called in <reference osisRef="1John.1.1">1Jo 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2</reference>, "the Word of Life."<div eID="gen28628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the life ... the light of men--</hi>All that in men which is true light--knowledge, integrity, intelligent, willing subjection to God, love to Him and to their fellow creatures, wisdom, purity, holy joy, rational happiness--all this "light of men" has its fountain in the essential original "life" of "the Word" (<reference osisRef="1John.1.5-1John.1.7">1Jo 1:5-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.9">Psa 36:9</reference>). <div eID="gen28629" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf175f08ce812170d610fcdecde3ca708efe5ded: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14831"/><div sID="gen28630" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14831"/><hi type="bold">5. shineth in darkness, &c.--</hi>in this dark, fallen world, or in mankind "sitting in darkness and the shadow of death," with no ability to find the way either of truth or of holiness. In this thick darkness, and consequent intellectual and moral obliquity, "the light of the Word" shineth--by all the rays whether of natural or revealed teaching which men (apart from the Incarnation of the Word) are favored with.<div eID="gen28630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the darkness comprehended it not--</hi>did not take it in, a brief summary of the effect of all the strivings of this unincarnate Word throughout this wide world from the beginning, and a hint of the necessity of His putting on flesh, if any recovery of men was to be effected (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">1Co 1:21</reference>). <div eID="gen28631" type="x-p"/>
entries.46abe43ef83716d7df2e375bb34dac570d846b80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14832"/><div sID="gen28632" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14832"/>6-9. The Evangelist here approaches his grand thesis, so paving his way for the full statement of it in <reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>, that we may be able to bear the bright light of it, and take in its length and breadth and depth and height. <div eID="gen28632" type="x-p"/>
entries.485b5c6af5f80311f2eb00ba19cd90bd923f0314: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14836"/><div sID="gen28636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14836"/><hi type="bold">10-13. He was in the world, &c.--</hi>The language here is nearly as wonderful as the thought. Observe its compact simplicity, its sonorousness--"the world" resounding in each of its three members--and the enigmatic form in which it is couched, startling the reader and setting his ingenuity a-working to solve the stupendous enigma of Christ ignored in His own world. "The world," in the first two clauses, plainly means the created world, into which He came, says <reference osisRef="John.1.9">Joh 1:9</reference>; "in it He was," says this verse. By His Incarnation, He became an inhabitant of it, and bound up with it. Yet it "was made by Him" (<reference osisRef="John.1.3-John.1.5">Joh 1:3-5</reference>). Here, then, it is merely alluded to, in contrast partly with His being in it, but still more with the reception He met with from it. "The world that knew Him not" (<reference osisRef="1John.3.1">1Jo 3:1</reference>) is of course the intelligent world of mankind. (See on <reference osisRef="John.1.11">Joh 1:11</reference>,<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>). Taking the first two clauses as one statement, we try to apprehend it by thinking of the infant Christ conceived in the womb and born in the arms of His own creature, and of the Man Christ Jesus breathing His own air, treading His own ground, supported by substances to which He Himself gave being, and the Creator of the very men whom He came to save. But the most vivid commentary on this entire verse will be got by tracing (in His matchless history) Him of whom it speaks walking amidst all the elements of nature, the diseases of men and death itself, the secrets of the human heart, and "the rulers of the darkness of this world" in all their number, subtlety, and malignity, not only with absolute ease, as their conscious Lord, but, as we might say, with full consciousness on their part of the presence of their Maker, whose will to one and all of them was law. And this is He of whom it is added, "the world knew Him not!" <div eID="gen28636" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ad997773acbaf0ad70ed83d74a7afc4e01c978e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14840"/><div sID="gen28648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14840"/><hi type="bold">14. And the Word, &c.--</hi>To raise the reader to the altitude of this climax were the thirteen foregoing verses written.<div eID="gen28648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was made flesh--</hi>BECAME MAN, in man's present frail, mortal condition, denoted by the word "flesh" (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Is 40:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.24">1Pe 1:24</reference>). It is directed probably against the Docetæ, who held that Christ was not really but only apparently man; against whom this gentle spirit is vehement in his Epistles (<reference osisRef="1John.4.3">1Jo 4:3</reference>; 2Jo 7, 10, 11), [Lucke, &c.]. Nor could He be too much so, for with the verity of the Incarnation all substantial Christianity vanishes. But now, married to our nature, henceforth He is as personally conscious of all that is strictly human as of all that is properly divine; and our nature is in His Person redeemed and quickened, ennobled and transfigured.<div eID="gen28649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and dwelt--</hi>tabernacled or pitched his tent; a word peculiar to John, who uses it four times, all in the sense of a permanent stay (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.15">Re 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.12">12:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.6">13:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">21:3</reference>). For ever wedded to our "flesh," He has entered this tabernacle to "go no more out." The allusion is to that tabernacle where dwelt the Shekinah (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Mt 23:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.39">39</reference>), or manifested "Glory of the Lord," and with reference to God's permanent dwelling among His people (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.11">Le 26:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Psa 68:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.132.13">132:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.27">Eze 37:27</reference>). This is put almost beyond doubt by what immediately follows, "And we beheld his glory" [Lucke, Meyer, De Wette which last critic, rising higher than usual, says that thus were perfected all former partial manifestations of God in an essentially Personal and historically Human manifestation].<div eID="gen28650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">full of grace and truth--</hi>So it should read: "He dwelt among us full of grace and truth"; or, in Old Testament phrase, "Mercy and truth," denoting the whole fruit of God's purposes of love towards sinners of mankind, which until now existed only in promise, and the fulfilment at length of that promise in Christ; in one great word, "the SURE MERCIES of David" (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.34">Ac 13:34</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>). In His Person all that Grace and Truth which had been floating so long in shadowy forms, and darting into the souls of the poor and needy its broken beams, took everlasting possession of human flesh and filled it full. By this Incarnation of Grace and Truth, the teaching of thousands of years was at once transcended and beggared, and the family of God sprang into Manhood.<div eID="gen28651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and we beheld his glory--</hi>not by the eye of sense, which saw in Him only "the carpenter." His glory was "spiritually discerned" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7-1Cor.2.15">1Co 2:7-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.16">5:16</reference>)--the glory of surpassing grace, love, tenderness, wisdom, purity, spirituality; majesty and meekness, richness and poverty, power and weakness, meeting together in unique contrast; ever attracting and at times ravishing the "babes" that followed and forsook all for Him.<div eID="gen28652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the glory as of the only begotten of the Father--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Luke.1.35">Lu 1:35</reference>); not like, but "such as (belongs to)," such as became or was befitting the only begotten of the Father [Chrysostom in Lucke, Calvin, &c.], according to a well-known use of the word "as." <div eID="gen28653" type="x-p"/>
entries.359e27b4daec2f90207ec737fd344ee12a741571: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14841"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.1.15">Joh 1:15</reference>. A Saying of the Baptist Confirmatory of This.</title> <div sID="gen28654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14841"/><hi type="bold">15. after me--</hi>in official manifestation.<div eID="gen28654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before me--</hi>in rank and dignity.<div eID="gen28655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for he was before me--</hi>in existence; "His goings forth being from of old, from everlasting" (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mi 5:2</reference>). (Anything lower than this His words cannot mean); that is, "My Successor is my Superior, for He was my Predecessor." This enigmatic play upon the different senses of the words "before" and "after" was doubtless employed by the Baptist to arrest attention, and rivet the thought; and the Evangelist introduces it just to clinch his own statements. <div eID="gen28656" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed815a967b02cfd2d37a65d02804bdd50edae4dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14842"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.1.16-John.1.18">Joh 1:16-18</reference>. Same Subject Continued.</title> <div sID="gen28657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14842"/><hi type="bold">16. of his fulness--</hi>of "grace and truth," resuming the thread of <reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>.<div eID="gen28657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grace for grace--</hi>that is, grace upon grace (so all the best interpreters), in successive communications and larger measures, as each was able to take it in. Observe, the word "truth" is here dropped. "Grace" being the chosen New Testament word for the whole fulness of the new covenant, all that dwells in Christ for men. <div eID="gen28658" type="x-p"/>
entries.23e5bf9eadb6b8c95220a0cad95f13dd554454d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14843"/><div sID="gen28659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14843"/><hi type="bold">17. For, &c.--</hi>The Law elicits the consciousness of sin and the need of redemption; it only typifies the reality. The Gospel, on the contrary, actually communicates reality and power from above (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.6.14">Ro 6:14</reference>). Hence Paul terms the Old Testament "shadow," while he calls the New Testament "substance" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.17">Col 2:17</reference>) [Olshausen]. <div eID="gen28659" type="x-p"/>
entries.8cecb2f963f4946539ae5d188db43507e8b40369: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14844"/><div sID="gen28660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14844"/><hi type="bold">18. No man--</hi>"No one," in the widest sense.<div eID="gen28660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath seen God--</hi>by immediate gaze, or direct intuition.<div eID="gen28661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the bosom of the Father--</hi>A remarkable expression, used only here, presupposing the Son's conscious existence distinct from the Father, and expressing His immediate and most endeared access to, and absolute acquaintance with, Him.<div eID="gen28662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>emphatic; As if he should say, "He and He only hath declared Him," because He only can. <div eID="gen28663" type="x-p"/>
entries.772c4088f19cba8602381b760d90b78681d2c12a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14845"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.1.19-John.1.36">Joh 1:19-36</reference>. The Baptist's Testimony to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen28664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14845"/><hi type="bold">19. record--</hi>testimony.<div eID="gen28664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Jews--</hi>that is, the heads of the nation, the members of the Sanhedrim. In this peculiar sense our Evangelist seems always to use the term. <div eID="gen28665" type="x-p"/>
entries.f756d51f729515e80f044beb9b89f65f17bf99c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14846"/><div sID="gen28666" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14846"/><hi type="bold">20. confessed, &c.--</hi>that is, While many were ready to hail him as the Christ, he neither gave the slightest ground for such views, nor the least entertainment to them. <div eID="gen28666" type="x-p"/>
entries.667f91d5ddb87adfb750a22d456ec972f1b3c345: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14847"/><div sID="gen28667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14847"/><hi type="bold">21. Elias--</hi>in His own proper person.<div eID="gen28667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that prophet--</hi>announced in <reference osisRef="Deut.18.15">De 18:15</reference>, &c., about whom they seem not to have been agreed whether he were the same with the Messiah or no. <div eID="gen28668" type="x-p"/>
entries.e63c3b80d0428204d23476da496f41188e968eb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14848"/><div sID="gen28669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14848"/><hi type="bold">25. Why baptizest thou, if not, &c.--</hi>Thinking he disclaimed any special connection with Messiah's kingdom, they demand his right to gather disciples by baptism. <div eID="gen28669" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7965f4673d308578c4be3f0660493d024c5c161: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14849"/><div sID="gen28670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14849"/><hi type="bold">26. there standeth--</hi>This must have been spoken after the baptism of Christ, and possibly just after His temptation (see on <reference osisRef="John.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference>). <div eID="gen28670" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b5f298a7115ec500be9f8cec809d9367f79c164: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14850"/><div sID="gen28671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14850"/><hi type="bold">28. Bethabara--</hi>Rather, "Bethany" (according to nearly all the best and most ancient manuscripts); not the Bethany of Lazarus, but another of the same name, and distinguished from it as lying "beyond Jordan," on the east. <div eID="gen28671" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e5691faf0e5953d7f7f5e4a4eba8121d4519e97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14851"/><div sID="gen28672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14851"/><hi type="bold">29. seeth Jesus--</hi>fresh, probably, from the scene of the temptation.<div eID="gen28672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">coming unto him--</hi>as to congenial company (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.23">Ac 4:23</reference>), and to receive from him His first greeting.<div eID="gen28673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and saith--</hi>catching a sublime inspiration at the sight of Him approaching.<div eID="gen28674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lamb of God--</hi>the one God-ordained, God-gifted sacrificial offering.<div eID="gen28675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that taketh away--</hi>taketh up and taketh away. The word signifies both, as does the corresponding Hebrew word. Applied to sin, it means to be chargeable with the guilt of it (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.38">Ex 28:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.5.1">Le 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.20">Eze 18:20</reference>), and to bear it away (as often). In the Levitical victims both ideas met, as they do in Christ, the people's guilt being viewed as transferred to them, avenged in their death, and so borne away by them (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.15">Le 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.16.15">16:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.22">21, 22</reference>; and compare <reference osisRef="Isa.53.6-Isa.53.12">Is 53:6-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>).<div eID="gen28676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sin--</hi>The singular number being used to mark the collective burden and all-embracing efficacy.<div eID="gen28677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the world--</hi>not of Israel only, for whom the typical victims were exclusively offered. Wherever there shall live a sinner throughout the wide world, sinking under that burden too heavy for him to bear, he shall find in this "Lamb of God," a shoulder equal to the weight. The right note was struck at the first--balm, doubtless, to Christ's own spirit; nor was ever after, or ever will be, a more glorious utterance. <div eID="gen28678" type="x-p"/>
entries.b93ac1a66539ed9e8de9eaacb276bc7ce505c976: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14852"/><div sID="gen28679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14852"/><hi type="bold">31-34. knew him not--</hi>Living mostly apart, the one at Nazareth, the other in the Judean desert--to prevent all appearance of collusion, John only knew that at a definite time after his own call, his Master would show Himself. As He drew near for baptism one day, the last of all the crowd, the spirit of the Baptist heaving under a divine presentiment that the moment had at length arrived, and an air of unwonted serenity and dignity, not without traits, probably, of the family features, appearing in this Stranger, the Spirit said to him as to Samuel of his youthful type, "Arise, anoint Him, for this is He!" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.12">1Sa 16:12</reference>). But the sign which he was told to expect was the visible descent of the Spirit upon Him as He emerged out of the baptismal water. Then, catching up the voice from heaven, "he saw and bare record that this is the Son of God." <div eID="gen28679" type="x-p"/>
entries.2db90be7ab435d734501c7775db44ad0684c5eee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14853"/><div sID="gen28680" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14853"/><hi type="bold">35. John stood--</hi>"was standing," at his accustomed place. <div eID="gen28680" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b1182bc73687269c7e688caca4a53e549c57b89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14854"/><div sID="gen28681" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14854"/><hi type="bold">36. looking--</hi>having fixed his eyes, with significant gaze, on Jesus.<div eID="gen28681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as he walked--</hi>but not now to him. To have done this once (see on <reference osisRef="John.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference>) was humility enough [Bengel].<div eID="gen28682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Behold, &c.--</hi>The repetition of that wonderful proclamation, in identical terms and without another word, could only have been meant as a gentle hint to go after Him--as they did. <div eID="gen28683" type="x-p"/>
entries.88372b6fc7d353179b879bb5e29db28d34dd59f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14855"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.1.37-John.1.51">Joh 1:37-51</reference>. First Gathering of Disciples--John Andrew, Simon, Philip, Nathanael.</title> <div sID="gen28684" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14855"/><hi type="bold">38. What seek ye--</hi>gentle, winning question, remarkable as the Redeemer's first public utterance. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.12.18-Matt.12.20">Mt 12:18-20</reference>.)<div eID="gen28684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">where dwellest thou--</hi>that is, "That is a question we cannot answer in a moment; but had we Thy company for a calm hour in private, gladly should we open our burden." <div eID="gen28685" type="x-p"/>
entries.800bf30a18a8a71e9fa4494b9ea99d3c0dc434f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14856"/><div sID="gen28686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14856"/><hi type="bold">39. Come and see--</hi>His second utterance, more winning still.<div eID="gen28686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tenth hour--</hi>not ten A.M. (as some), according to Roman, but four P.M., according to Jewish reckoning, which John follows. The hour is mentioned to show why they stayed out the day with him--because little of it remained. <div eID="gen28687" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd2c397231442ad85f3d9268f1ede9ea6c29fc3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14857"/><div sID="gen28688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14857"/><hi type="bold">40. One ... was Andrew--</hi>The other was doubtless our Evangelist himself. His great sensitiveness is touchingly shown in his representation of this first contact with the Lord; the circumstances are present to him in the minutest details; he still remembers the Very hour. But "he reports no particulars of those discourses of the Lord by which he was bound to Him for the whole of His life; he allows everything personal to retire" [Olshausen].<div eID="gen28688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Peter's brother--</hi>and the elder of the two. <div eID="gen28689" type="x-p"/>
entries.b044a8f4c89b74cf997d6714315d9d7cc0f155db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14858"/><div sID="gen28690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14858"/><hi type="bold">41. have found the Messias--</hi>The previous preparation of their simple hearts under the Baptist's ministry, made quick work of this blessed conviction, while others hesitated till doubt settled into obduracy. So it is still. <div eID="gen28690" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ef085f7e2c8947b21b575f7399827780fd3223f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14859"/><div sID="gen28691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14859"/><hi type="bold">42. brought him to Jesus--</hi>Happy brothers that thus do to each other!<div eID="gen28691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beheld him--</hi>fixed his eyes on him, with significant gaze (as <reference osisRef="John.1.36">Joh 1:36</reference>).<div eID="gen28692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Cephas ... stone--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Mt 16:18</reference>). <div eID="gen28693" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8016cfca2a42245f575c2197a2cebf9f5f9e669: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14860"/><div sID="gen28694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14860"/><hi type="bold">43. would go ... into Galilee--</hi>for from His baptism He had sojourned in Judea (showing that the calling at the Sea of Galilee [Mt 4:18] was a subsequent one, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.5.1">Lu 5:1</reference>).<div eID="gen28694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Follow me--</hi>the first express call given, the former three having come to Him spontaneously. <div eID="gen28695" type="x-p"/>
entries.020bcc6d2d33cda93ce88058a4c3a0941560aa86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14861"/><div sID="gen28696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14861"/><hi type="bold">44. the city of Andrew and Peter--</hi>of their birth probably, for they seem to have lived at Capernaum (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.29">Mr 1:29</reference>). <div eID="gen28696" type="x-p"/>
entries.20201f44e81da98b7073e964ae2df535f12dca96: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14862"/><div sID="gen28697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14862"/><hi type="bold">45. Nathanael--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.3">Mt 10:3</reference>).<div eID="gen28697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Moses--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="John.5.46">Joh 5:46</reference>).<div eID="gen28698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Joseph--</hi>the current way of speaking. (See <reference osisRef="Luke.3.23">Lu 3:23</reference>). <div eID="gen28699" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8aa1ee033533a46a74c41d04ef807e2259ce484: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14863"/><div sID="gen28700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14863"/><hi type="bold">46. any good out of Nazareth--</hi>remembering Bethlehem, perhaps, as Messiah's predicted birthplace, and Nazareth having no express prophetic place at all, besides being in no repute. The question sprang from mere dread of mistake in a matter so vital.<div eID="gen28700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Come and see--</hi>Noble remedy against preconceived opinions [Bengel]. Philip, though he could not perhaps solve his difficulty, could show him how to get rid of it. (See on <reference osisRef="John.6.68">Joh 6:68</reference>). <div eID="gen28701" type="x-p"/>
entries.a142285eddf1c9afd1981b41a8cff1f89adc40dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14864"/><div sID="gen28702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14864"/><hi type="bold">47. an Israelite indeed ... no guile--</hi>not only no hypocrite, but with a guileless simplicity not always found even in God's own people, ready to follow wherever truth might lead him, saying, Samuel-like, "Speak, Lord, for Thy servant heareth" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.10">1Sa 3:10</reference>). <div eID="gen28702" type="x-p"/>
entries.e118db840cf380221d30e41ad104873fc33406dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14865"/><div sID="gen28703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14865"/><hi type="bold">48. Whence knowest thou me--</hi>conscious that his very heart had been read, and at this critical moment more than ever before.<div eID="gen28703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Before Philip called thee--</hi>showing He knew all that passed between Philip and him at a distance.<div eID="gen28704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when ... under the fig tree, &c.--</hi>where retirement for meditation and prayer was not uncommon [Lightfoot]. Thither, probably--hearing that his master's Master had at length appeared, and heaving with mingled eagerness to behold Him and dread of deception--he had retired to pour out his guileless heart for light and guidance, ending with such a prayer as this, "Show me a token for good!" (See on <reference osisRef="Luke.2.8">Lu 2:8</reference>). Now he has it, "Thou guileless one, that fig tree scene, with all its heaving anxieties, deep pleadings and tremulous hopes--I saw it all." The first words of Jesus had astonished, but this quite overpowered and won him. <div eID="gen28705" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa1b618da6183c89a48a82a06ed657679079c0e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14866"/><div sID="gen28706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14866"/><hi type="bold">49. Son of God ... King of Israel--</hi>the one denoting His person, the other His office. How much loftier this than anything Philip had said to him! But just as the earth's vital powers, the longer they are frost-bound, take the greater spring when at length set free, so souls, like Nathanael and Thomas (see on <reference osisRef="John.20.28">Joh 20:28</reference>), the outgoings of whose faith are hindered for a time, take the start of their more easy-going brethren when loosed and let go. <div eID="gen28706" type="x-p"/>
entries.e753a0a5c40c154246409e37a2fae4177922aee1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14867"/><div sID="gen28707" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14867"/><hi type="bold">50-51. Because I said, &c.--</hi>"So quickly convinced, and on this evidence only?"--an expression of admiration. <div eID="gen28707" type="x-p"/>

entries.a351488bd09ad80b9248cfdfeae3de6c7717972f: <div eID="gen41314" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Gospel According to St. John With A Short Account of His Life</title> <div sID="gen41315" type="x-p"/> John, the writer of this Gospel, was the son of a fisherman named Zebedee, and his mother's name was Salome. Compare <reference osisRef="Mat.27.56">Mat 27:56</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Mar.15.40">Mar 15:40</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Mar.16.1">Mar 16:1</reference>. His father Zebedee was probably of Bethsaida, and with his sons James and John followed his occupation on the sea of Galilee. The call of these two brothers to the apostleship is related, <reference osisRef="Mat.4.21">Mat 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.4.22">Mat 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.1.19">Mar 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.20">Mar 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.5.1-Luk.5.10">Luk 5:1-10</reference>. John is generally supposed to have been about 25 years of age when he began to follow our Lord. <div eID="gen41315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41316" type="x-p"/> Theophylact makes him one of the relatives of our Lord, and gives his genealogy thus: "Joseph, the husband of the blessed Mary, had seven children by a former wife, four sons and three daughters-Martha, (perhaps, says Dr. Lardner, it should be Mary), Esther, and Salome, whose son John was; therefore Salome was reckoned out Lord's sister, and John was his nephew." If this relationship did exist, it may have been, at least in part, the reason of several things mentioned in the Gospels: as the petition of the two brothers for the two chief places in the kingdom of Christ; John's being the beloved disciple and friend of Jesus, and being admitted to some familiarities denied to the rest, and possibly performing some offices about the person of his Master; and, finally, our Lord's committing to him the care of his mother, as long as she should survive him. In a MS. of the Greek Testament in the Imperial Library of Vienna, numbered 34 in Lambecius's Catalogue, there is a marginal note which agrees pretty much with the account given above by Theophylact: viz. "John the evangelist was cousin to our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh: for Joseph, the spouse of the God-bearing virgin, had four sons by his own wife, James, Simon, Jude, and Joses, and three daughters, Esther, and Thamar, and a third who, with her mother, was called Salome, who was given by Joseph in marriage to Zebedee: of her, Zebedee begot James, and John also the evangelist." The writer of the MS. professes to have taken this account from the commentaries of St Sophronius. <div eID="gen41316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41317" type="x-p"/> This evangelist is supposed by some to have been the bridegroom at the marriage of Cana in Galilee: see <reference osisRef="Joh.2.1">Joh 2:1</reference>. <div eID="gen41317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41318" type="x-p"/> John was with our Lord in his transfiguration on the mount, <reference osisRef="Mat.17.2">Mat 17:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.9.2">Mar 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.9.28">Luk 9:28</reference>; during his agony in the garden, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.37">Mat 26:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.14.33">Mar 14:33</reference>; and when he was crucified, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.26">Joh 19:26</reference>. <div eID="gen41318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41319" type="x-p"/> He saw our Lord expire upon the cross, and saw the soldier pierce his side with a spear, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.34">Joh 19:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.35">Joh 19:35</reference>. <div eID="gen41319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41320" type="x-p"/> He was one of the first of the disciples that visited the sepulchre after the resurrection of Christ; and was present with the other disciples, when Jesus showed himself to them on the evening of the same day on which he arose; and likewise eight days after, <reference osisRef="Joh.20.19-Joh.20.29">Joh 20:19-29</reference>. <div eID="gen41320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41321" type="x-p"/> In conjunction with Peter, he cured a man who had been lame from his mother's womb, for which he was cast into prison, <reference osisRef="Act.3.1-Act.3.10">Act 3:1-10</reference>. He was afterwards sent to Samaria, to confer the Holy Ghost on those who had been converted there by Philip the deacon, Acts 8:5-25. St. Paul informs us, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.9">Gal 2:9</reference>, that John was present at the council of Jerusalem, of which an account is given, <reference osisRef="Act.15.4">Act 15:4</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen41321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41322" type="x-p"/> It is evident that John was present at most of the things related by him in his Gospel; and that he was an eye and ear witness of our Lord's labors, journeyings, discourses, miracles, passion; crucifixion, resurrection, and ascension. After the ascension he returned with the other apostles from mount Olivet to Jerusalem, and took part in all transactions previously to the day of pentecost: on which time, he, with the rest, partook of the mighty outpouring of the Holy Spirit, by which he was eminently qualified for the place he afterwards held in the apostolic Church. <div eID="gen41322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41323" type="x-p"/> Some of the ancients believed that he went into Parthia, and preached the Gospel there; and his first epistle has been sometimes cited under the name of the Epistle to the Parthians. <div eID="gen41323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41324" type="x-p"/> Irenaeus, Eusebius, Origen, and others, assert that he was a long tune in Asia, continuing there till Trajan's time, who succeeded Nerva, a.d. 98. And Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, a.d. 196, asserts that John was buried in that city. Jerome confirms this testimony, and says that John's death happened in the 68th year after our Lord's passion. <div eID="gen41324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41325" type="x-p"/> Tertullian and others say that Domitian having declared war against the Church of Christ, in the 15th year of his reign, a.d. 95, John was banished from Ephesus, and carried to Rome, where he was immersed in a cauldron of boiling oil, out of which however he escaped unhurt; and that afterwards he was banished to the isle of Patmos, in the Aegean Sea, where he wrote the Apocalypse. Domitian having been slain in a.d. 96, his successor Nerva recalled all the exiles who had been banished by his predecessor; and John is supposed to have returned the next year to Ephesus, being then about ninety years of age. He is thought to have been the only apostle who died a natural death, and to have lived upwards of 100 years. Some say, having completed 100 years, he died the day following. This Gospel is supposed by learned men to have been written about a.d. 68 or 70; by others, a.d. 86; and, by others, a.d. 97; but the most probable opinion is that it was written at Ephesus about the year 86. <div eID="gen41325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41326" type="x-p"/> Jerome, in his comment on Galatians 6, says that John continued preaching when he was so enfeebled with old age that he was obliged to be carried into the assembly; and that, not being able to deliver any long discourse, his custom was to say, in every meeting, My dear children, love one another! The holy virgin lived under his care till the day of her death, which is supposed to have taken place fifteen years after the crucifixion. <div eID="gen41326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41327" type="x-p"/> John is usually painted holding a cup in his hand, with a serpent issuing from it: this took its rise from a relation by the spurious Procorus, who styles himself a disciple of St. John. Though the story is not worth relating, curiosity will naturally wish to be gratified with it. Some heretics had privately poisoned a cup of liquor, with which they presented him; but after he had prayed to God, and made the sign of the cross over it, the venom was expelled, in the form of a serpent! <div eID="gen41327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41328" type="x-p"/> Some of the first disciples of our Lord, misunderstanding the passage, <reference osisRef="Joh.21.22">Joh 21:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.21.23">Joh 21:23</reference>, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? believed that John should never die. Several in the primitive Church were of the same opinion; and to this day his death is doubted by persons of the first repute for piety and morality. Where such doctors disagree, it would be thought presumption in me to attempt to decide; otherwise I should not have hesitated to say that, seventeen hundred years ago he went the way of all flesh, and, instead of a wandering lot in a miserable, perishing world, is now glorified in that heaven of which his writings prove he had so large an anticipation, both before and after the crucifixion of his Lord. <div eID="gen41328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41329" type="x-p"/> Eusebius (Hist. Eccles. lib. iii. cap. 24) treats particularly of the order of the Gospels, and especially of this evangelist: his observations are of considerable importance, and deserve a place here. Dr. Lardner has quoted him at large, Works, vol. iv. p. 224. "Let us," says he, "observe the writings of this apostle which are not contradicted by any. And first of all must be mentioned, as acknowledged of all, the Gospel according to him, well known to all the Churches under heaven. And that it has been justly placed by the ancients the fourth in order, and after the other three, may be made evident in this manner. Those admirable and truly Divine men, the apostles of Christ, eminently holy in their lives, and, as to their minds, adorned with every virtue, but rude in language, confiding in the Divine and miraculous power bestowed upon them by our Savior, neither knew, nor attempted to deliver the doctrine of their Master with the artifice and eloquence of words. But using only the demonstration of the Divine Spirit, working with them, and the power of Christ performing by them many miracles, they spread the knowledge of the kingdom of heaven all over the world. Nor were they greatly concerned about the writing of books, being engaged in a more excellent ministry, which was above all human power. Insomuch that Paul, the most able of all in the furniture both of words and thoughts, has left nothing in writing, beside some very short (or a very few) epistles; although he was acquainted with innumerable mysteries, having been admitted to the sight and contemplation of things in the third heaven, and been caught up into the Divine Paradise, and there allowed to hear unspeakable words. Nor were the rest of our Savior's followers unacquainted with these things, as the seventy disciples, and many other beside the twelve apostles. Nevertheless, of all the disciples of our Lord, Matthew and John only have left us any memoirs: who too, as we have been informed, were compelled to write by a kind of necessity. For Matthew having first preached to the Hebrews, when he was about to go to other people, delivered to them in their own language the Gospel according to him, by that writing supplying the want of his presence with those whom he was then leaving. And when Mark and Luke had published the Gospels according to them, it is said that John, who all this while had preached by word of mouth, was at length induced to write for this reason. The three first written Gospels being now delivered to all men, and to John himself, it is said that he approved them, and confirmed the truth of their narration by his own testimony; saying there was only wanting a written account of the things done by Christ in the former part, and the beginning of his preaching. And certainly that observation is very true. For it is easy to perceive that the other three evangelists have recorded only the actions of our Savior for one year after the imprisonment of John, as they themselves declare at the beginning of their history. For, after mentioning the forty days' fast, and the succeeding temptation, Matthew shows the time of the commencement of his account in these words: When he had heard that John was cast into prison, he departed out of Judea into Galilee. In like manner, Mark: Now after that John, says he, was cast into prison, Jesus came into Galilee. And Luke, before he begins the account of the acts of Jesus, gives a like hint in this manner: that Herod added yet this, above all, that he shut up John in prison. For these reasons, as is said, the Apostle John was entreated to relate, in the Gospel according to him, the time omitted by the four evangelists, and the things done by our Savior in that space, before the imprisonment of the Baptist; And they add, farther, that he himself hints as much, saying, This beginning of miracles did Jesus: as also in the history of the acts of Jesus he makes mention of the Baptist as still baptizing in Aenon, nigh unto Salem. And it is thought that he expressly declares as much, when he says, For John was not yet cast into prison. John, therefore, in the Gospel according to him, relates the things done by Christ while the Baptist was not yet cast into prison. But the other three evangelists relate the things that followed the Baptist's confinement. Whoever attends to these things will not any longer think the evangelists disagree with each other, forasmuch as the Gospel according to John contains the first actions of Christ, while the others give the history of the following time. And for the same reason John has omitted the genealogy of our Savior according to the flesh, it having been recorded before by Matthew and Luke; but he begins with his divinity, which had been reserved by the Holy Ghost for him, as the most excellent person." The whole of this chapter, with the preceding and following, may be profitably consulted by the reader. See also Lardner, Works, vol. iv. 224, and vi. 156-222. <div eID="gen41329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41330" type="x-p"/> Besides the Gospel before us, John is generally reputed to have been the author of the three epistles which go under his name, and of the Apocalypse. The former certainly breathe the genuine spirit of this apostle; and are invaluable monuments of his spiritual knowledge and deep piety, as well as of his Divine inspiration: as the Gospel and Epistles prove him to have been an evangelist and apostle, his book of Revelations ranks him among the profoundest of the prophets. <div eID="gen41330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41331" type="x-p"/> Learned men are not wholly agreed about the language in which this Gospel was originally written. Some think St. John wrote it in his own native tongue, the Aramean or Syriac, and that it was afterwards translated, by rather an unskilful hand, into Greek. This opinion is not supported by strong arguments. That it was originally written in Greek is the general and most likely opinion. <div eID="gen41331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41332" type="x-p"/> What the design of St. John was, in writing this Gospel, has divided and perplexed many critics and learned divines. Some suppose that it was to refute the errors taught by one Cerinthus, who rose up at that time, and asserted that Jesus was not born of a virgin, but was the real son of Joseph and Mary; that, at his baptism, the Christ, what we term the Divine nature, descended into him, in the form of a dove, by whose influence he worked all his miracles; and that, when he was about to suffer, this Christ, or Divine nature, departed from him, and left the man Jesus to suffer death. See Irenaeus, advers.
