This in <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> seems ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther to be a Prophecy than a <ns0:hi>Call.</ns0:hi> Those Texts, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 4.18, 19, 20. and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 5.10. seem to be their calls to a Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scipleship; the other Texts, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 3.13. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 6.13. respects their Election to the Apostleship, and the mission of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 The day following Jesus would go forth in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to Galilee, and findeth Philip <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">All this while Christ seemeth to have been in <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> (which was the most famous Province); the day after <ns0:hi>Pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter</ns0:hi> had thus been with him, he had a mind to go into <ns0:hi>Gali<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lee</ns0:hi>; out of that he designed to choose his Disciples; and that being the Country where he had been Educated, he de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signed in a more special manner to honour it with the first Fruit of his publick Ministry; there he findeth <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> (the name signifieth a Lover of Horses.)</ns0:note>, and saith unto him, Follow me <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He calleth him to be his Disciple.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 Now <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 12.21.</ns0:note> Philip was of Bethsaida <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> was a Citizen of <ns0:hi>Bethsaida,</ns0:hi> (the word signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> the house of Fruits, or of Huntsmen.)</ns0:note>, the City of Andrew and Peter <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Andrew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> (mentioned before) both of them lived there: It was one of those Cities where Christ did most of his mighty Works, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11.20.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="45">45 Philip findeth Nathaneel <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> having himself discovered Christ, is not willing to eat his Morsels alone, but desires to communicate his discovery to others; he finds (whether casually, or upon search, is not said) one <ns0:hi>Nathaneel,</ns0:hi> he was one of <ns0:hi>Cana</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> ch. 21.2. (The name is an <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> name, signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fying, <ns0:hi>The Gift of God</ns0:hi>; some think it the same with <ns0:hi>Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thanael,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 15.24.)</ns0:note>, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 49.10. Deut. 18.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. See Luke <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.27.</ns0:note> Moses in the Law, and the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Isaiah 4<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 2. and 53.2. <ns0:hi>Mi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 5.2 Zech. 6.12<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and 9 9. more on L<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e 24 27.</ns0:note> Prophets did write <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Having found him, he tells him with great joy, that they had found him of whom <ns0:hi>Mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses</ns0:hi> had wrote in the Law, the <ns0:hi>Shilo</ns0:hi> mentioned, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 49.10. the Prophet mentioned, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 18.15. the <ns0:hi>branch of the Lord</ns0:hi> mentioned, <ns0:hi>Is.</ns0:hi> 4.2. the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> mentioned by <ns0:hi>Daniel, Dan.</ns0:hi> 9.25, 26. and all the other <ns0:hi>Prophets,</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, Jesus <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 2.23. Luke 2.4.</ns0:note> of Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zareth the Son of Joseph <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">him whom they usually called <ns0:hi>Iesus</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Nazareth,</ns0:hi> (there he was conceived, there he was bred, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 2.4, 51.) Though he was born in <ns0:hi>Bethlehem</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Iudah, v.</ns0:hi> 4. and who was commonly thought to be the Son of <ns0:hi>Ioseph.</ns0:hi> If <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> did only, <ns0:hi>cum vulgo loqui,</ns0:hi> speak as was commonly said, though himself knew and believed other things, he is not to be blamed: but the most think <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> discovered here his own weak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, both in thinking Christ the Son of <ns0:hi>Ioseph,</ns0:hi> and to have been born at <ns0:hi>Nazareth.</ns0:hi> It is certain, that the Apostles themselves at first, yea, and till Christ's Resurrection from the Dead, had a very imperfect Notion of Christ, as the true <ns0:hi>Messiah.</ns0:hi> Grace may consist with great weakness as to knowledge.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="46">46 And Nathaneel said unto him, Can there any good thing, come out of Nazareth <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The words of <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> begat a prejudice in <ns0:hi>Nathaneel,</ns0:hi> as to what he said. <ns0:hi>Micah</ns0:hi> 5.2. it was prophesied, that the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> should come out of <ns0:hi>Bethlehem.</ns0:hi> So ch. 7.41. Some of the people said, <ns0:hi>Shall Christ come out of Galilee? Hath not the Scripture said, that Christ cometh of the Seed of</ns0:hi> David, <ns0:hi>and out of the Town of</ns0:hi> Bethlehem, <ns0:hi>where</ns0:hi> David <ns0:hi>was? Nazareth</ns0:hi> was not only a poor little place, (for so <ns0:hi>Bethlehem</ns0:hi> also was) but a place which the Scripture ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver mentioned, as the place from whence the <ns0:hi>Messiah</ns0:hi> should arise; a place that God had not honoured with the production of a Prophet. By <ns0:hi>any good thing</ns0:hi> seems to be meant, the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> or any <ns0:hi>Prophet,</ns0:hi> or (more general<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly) any thing which is noble, and excellent, and of any re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mark: So prone are we to think, that the Kingdom of God comes with observation, that we know not how to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ancy how great things should be done by little means, and great persons should arise out of little contemptible places. Whereas God chuseth <ns0:hi>the foolish things of the World, to confound the wise; and the weak things to confound the migh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty; and base things of the World,</ns0:hi> to confound the Wise, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.25, 26, 27.</ns0:note>? Philip saith unto him, Come and see <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> not knowing how to an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swer <ns0:hi>Nathanael</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>objection,</ns0:hi> and to remove his prejudice, wisheth him himself to go, and make up a Judgment. Wise men ought to do this, and not to take up prejudices from reports and common <ns0:hi>Vogue.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 Jesus saw Nathaneel coming to him, and
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:330" />
saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">They are not all <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> which are of <ns0:hi>Israel, Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.6. <ns0:hi>For he is not a Iew, which is one outwardly: neither is that circumcision, which is outward, in the flesh: But he is a Iew which is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the Spirit, Rom.</ns0:hi> 2.28, 29. Christ seeing <ns0:hi>Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thanael</ns0:hi> (though he was prejudiced by <ns0:hi>Philips</ns0:hi> mistake, or the common mistake of his Nation) coming to see him, and seeing not onely his body and bodily motion, but his heart also, and the motions of that, saith of him, <ns0:hi>Behold</ns0:hi> one who is not onely born an <ns0:hi>Israelite,</ns0:hi> but is a true <ns0:hi>Israelite,</ns0:hi> like his Father <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>plain Man, Gen.</ns0:hi> 25.27.</ns0:note>, in whom is no guile <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">In whom there is no <ns0:hi>deceit,</ns0:hi> no doubleness of heart; such ought Christians to be, no crafty, deceitful, double-minded men, but men of great sincerity, and plainness of heart, <ns0:hi>laying aside all malice,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>all guile,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.1. like little Children, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 18.3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="48">48 Nathanael saith unto him, Whence knowest thou me <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Nathanael</ns0:hi> wondereth how Christ should know him, having not been of his familiar acquaintance;</ns0:note>? Jesus answered and said unto him, Before that Philip called thee, when thou wert under the Fig-tree, I saw thee <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Christ tells him, he saw him under the <ns0:hi>Fig-tree,</ns0:hi> before ever <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led him. That was a very hot Country, wherein people <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ought shadowy places; hence we read of sitting under their own <ns0:hi>Vines</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Fig-trees, Micah</ns0:hi> 4.4. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 3.10. and it is likely that those being two luxuriant plants, that had large Leaves, and ran out in long Boughs in hot Weather, they might under the covert of these Plants, not only sit as in an Arbour to converse one with another, but also perform Religious Duties. Whether Christ saw him there eating, and drinking, or conversing with friends, or reading, or pray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, the Scripture saith not, and it is but vainly guessed; it is enough that by his telling this to him, he let him know, that he saw him, though he was not in his view, and so was <ns0:hi>Omnipresent,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Omniscient.</ns0:hi> Christ seeth us where we are, and what we do, when we see not him; and he seeth our hearts, whether they be single, or double, plain, or false, and deceitful; which as in many cases it affordeth us much comfort, so it admonisheth us to be at all times in the fear of the Lord.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="49">49 Nathanael answered, and said unto him, Rabhi, thou art the Son of God <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The term <ns0:hi>Rabbi,</ns0:hi> which <ns0:hi>Nathanael</ns0:hi> here giveth to Christ, is of the same significancy with <ns0:hi>Rabban,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Rabbo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ni, Iohn</ns0:hi> 20.16. <ns0:hi>Rabban, Rabhi, Rabbi,</ns0:hi> all which signify Master, and my Master; a name which in that age they usually gave their Teachers, as a Title of <ns0:hi>Honour, Matth.</ns0:hi> 23.7, 8. titles that began about the time of our Saviour; for <ns0:hi>Buxtorf</ns0:hi> tells us, Purer antiquity gave no such Titles to their Teachers or Prophets, thinking it not possible to give those persons (extraordinarily sent of God) Titles answera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble to their Dignity; They say, <ns0:hi>Hillel</ns0:hi> about our Saviours time was the first who was so called; <ns0:hi>Rabban</ns0:hi> was counted the highest; <ns0:hi>Rabbi</ns0:hi> the next, <ns0:hi>Rabhi</ns0:hi> the least. <ns0:hi>Rabban,</ns0:hi> they say, lasted but two hundred years, given to seven after <ns0:hi>Hil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lel. Nathanael</ns0:hi> calls him also <ns0:hi>the Son of God,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Peter,</ns0:hi> and the other Disciples did, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 14.33. and <ns0:hi>Peter, Matth.</ns0:hi> 16.16. But it appeareth that they had but a faint perswasion of this, by many following passages, till he was declared so with power, by his Resurrection from the dead, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.4.</ns0:note>, thou art the King of Israel <ns0:hi>u.</ns0:hi>
                  <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He acknowledgeth Christ also the <ns0:hi>King of Israel,</ns0:hi> that is, the true <ns0:hi>Messiah.</ns0:hi> This was the title of the <ns0:hi>Messiah, Matth.</ns0:hi> 21.5. and 27.11.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="50">50 Jesus answered, and said unto him, Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig-tree, believest thou <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Christ incourageth the beginnings of faith in the Souls of his people, and magnifies <ns0:hi>Nathanael</ns0:hi>'s faith from the <ns0:hi>Revelation</ns0:hi> which he had, which was but imperfect; for Christ had said no more, than that he had seen him under the fig-tree, before <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> called him.</ns0:note>? thou shalt see greater things then these <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">He tells him that he should see greater things than these. <ns0:hi>To him that hath, shall be given.</ns0:hi> What those greater things are, which our Lord here meaneth, he telleth him (in part at least, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 51.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="51">51 And he saith unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto you <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">These things he ushers in with a <ns0:hi>Verily, verily,</ns0:hi> and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clareth them, spoken not to <ns0:hi>Nathanael</ns0:hi> alone, but <ns0:hi>to you; viz<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:hi> all you that are my Disciples indeed, who are (like <ns0:hi>Natha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nael</ns0:hi>), true <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> in whom there is no guile. For the terms, <ns0:hi>Amen, Amen,</ns0:hi> (by us translated, <ns0:hi>Verily, Verily</ns0:hi>) some of the Ancients, accounted them an Oath; but the most learned Modern Writers, have seen no reason to agree with them. Surely (see a large Discourse about these Particles in our learned <ns0:hi>Fuller,</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>Miscellan, l.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>cap.</ns0:hi> 2. to which nothing need be added) if <ns0:hi>Amen</ns0:hi> is never used in the <ns0:hi>Old Testament,</ns0:hi> but as a term of <ns0:hi>prayer</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>wishing</ns0:hi>; in the <ns0:hi>New Testament</ns0:hi> it is used to assert or affirm a thing, or as a <ns0:hi>particle</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>wishing</ns0:hi> and prayer. The word in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> properly signifies, <ns0:hi>Truth, Isa.</ns0:hi> 65.16. whence Christ (the Truth) is called the <ns0:hi>Amen, Rev.</ns0:hi> 3.14. As the Prophets were wont to begin their Discourses with <ns0:hi>The word of the Lord,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>thus saith the Lord,</ns0:hi> to assert the Truth of what they were about to say; So Christ, to shew that himself was God, and spake from himself, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gineth with <ns0:hi>Amen,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Amen, Amen</ns0:hi> sometimes; it is observed that <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> constantly doubles the particle, and saith <ns0:hi>Amen, Amen,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>Verily, Verily.</ns0:hi> Either (as In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpreters say) for further Confirmation of the thing, or to get the greater <ns0:hi>Attention,</ns0:hi> or to assert as well the truth of the <ns0:hi>Speaker,</ns0:hi> as of the <ns0:hi>thing spoken.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 4.11, 5. Luke 2.9, 13. and 22.43. and 24.4. Acts 1.10.</ns0:note>, Hereafter you shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scending upon the son of man <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">No<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> the thing spoken followeth as a thing promised, not to <ns0:hi>Nathanael</ns0:hi> only, but to all Believers, <ns0:hi>That they should see the heavens opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the son of man.</ns0:hi> Some think that here<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by is meant, the spiritual Metaphorical opening of Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven to Believers by Christ. But it seems more properly to signifie, such an opening of the Heavens as we read of<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 3.16. Some understand it of the appear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ances of Angels to Christ at his Passion, and Resurrection, and Ascention; but it seems rather to refer to the day of Judgment, when Ten thousands of Angels shall wait upon Christ, as the Judg of the Quick and the Dead, and Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nister unto him; which Ministration, they say, is expressed by the terms of Ascending and Descending, with reference (doubtless) to <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi>'s Vision, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 28.12. <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> saw it sleeping, <ns0:hi>Nathanael</ns0:hi> and other Believers shall see it with open Eyes. Others Interpret it more generally, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> You shall see as many Miracles, as if you saw the Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vens opened, and the <ns0:hi>Angels</ns0:hi> Ascending and Descend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing. Others think it referreth to some further appearances of the <ns0:hi>Angels</ns0:hi> to Christ in their Ministration to him, than the Scripture records. Christ doth not say, You shall see <ns0:hi>Angels</ns0:hi> Ascending and Descending upon me, but upon <ns0:hi>the Son of man</ns0:hi>; by which our learned <ns0:hi>Lightfoot</ns0:hi> saith, He did not only declare himself to be truly man, but the <ns0:hi>se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cond Adam,</ns0:hi> in whom what was lost in the first<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> was to be restored. It is observed, that onely <ns0:hi>Ezekiel</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>Old Testament,</ns0:hi> and Christ in the <ns0:hi>New Testament,</ns0:hi> are thus called; and that Christ was never thus called, but by himself; <ns0:hi>Ezekiel</ns0:hi> was doubtless so called, to distinguish him from those spiritual Beings with which he often con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versed. Christ, to distinguish his Humane Nature from his <ns0:hi>Divine Nature</ns0:hi>; both which (in him) made up one Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son. Christs calling himself so, was but a further Indi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cation of his making himself of <ns0:hi>no Reputation,</ns0:hi> while <ns0:hi>he was in the form of a Servant.</ns0:hi> Others think, that <ns0:hi>the Son of man</ns0:hi> in the Gospel used by Christ, signifies no more than <ns0:hi>I,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>me</ns0:hi>; (it being usual in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew Dialect</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> for Persons to speak of themselves in the third person); so <ns0:hi>upon the Son of man,</ns0:hi> is upon me, who am truly man. <ns0:hi>Chemnitius</ns0:hi> thinks, that as the term <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> (by which the people commonly called Christ) was taken out of <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi>; So this term by Christ applyed to the same Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, is taken out thence too, <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 7.13. Where it is said, one <ns0:hi>like the son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days,</ns0:hi> &c. And that Christ did ordinarily so call himself, to correspond with the <ns0:hi>Prophe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy of Daniel,</ns0:hi> to assert himself truly man, and to declare himself his Fathers <ns0:hi>Servant,</ns0:hi> according to the Prophecy<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 42.1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
